- Water & Environmental
heading: Case Studies

text:
Why CFD?

Why do we use Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)? The basic reason is that computer simulations can do things that experiments and mathematical analysis cannot. Once validated as a source of decent approximations of physical observations, a numerical simulation program can provide detailed information about a fluid flow problem, such as densities, pressures, temperatures and velocities throughout a flow. Initial and boundary conditions can be easily modified, and the consequences readily evaluated. These are the obvious things that make CFD useful. But there are more fundamental reasons for using CFD. In the following paragraphs, examples are used to show why CFD is fundamentally important. This presentation is only focused on fluid dynamics, but some of the reasons for computational analysis of fluids also applies to other kinds of continuum dynamics.
heading: Why CFD?

text:
Why CFD? > Modeling fuel sloshing in spacecraft

In spacecraft containing liquid fuel tanks, the fuel can slosh, causing unwanted forces that can interfere with the motion of the craft, as well as making the fuel difficult to access for powering the control jets. This sloshing in space, where there is little or no gravity, is a situation that cannot be duplicated with experiments on earth. In a computational simulation however, the magnitude of gravity can be set to any value, including zero. This, then is a situation where there is little or no alternative for studying the dynamics of liquid fuels in space craft. A good example of this is illustrated in the 2017 ***FLOW-3D*** User Conference presentation, “Modelling of upper stage dynamics including fuel sloshing,” by Francesco De Rose at Airbus Safran Launchers.
heading: Why CFD? > Modeling fuel sloshing in spacecraft

text:
Why CFD? > Liquid behavior in inkjet printers

A somewhat different problem will be familiar to most of us. Your computer may have a printer connected to it. Most often that printer uses inkjet technology, in which tiny jets of liquid ink are shot at a sheet of paper. These jets have a very small diameter (typically less than 60µm) and are designed to break up into tiny drops that are directed to form a pattern on paper. In many cases there may be multiple jets operating to speed up the printing process. Creating jets can be done in several ways using pressure pulses, moving diaphragms, pistons, etc. Once ink has been ejected from a nozzle, the chamber containing the ink must be quickly refilled so that another jet can be generated.

Because of their small size, and the short time of existence of an inkjet, it is difficult to observe the liquid behavior of pinch off and breakup of the jets. Furthermore, the fluid dynamics inside the mechanism that generates the jet cannot be observed in laboratory experiments. Instead, computational simulations can reveal the workings of inkjets in considerable detail, making the development of faster and more accurate printing possible. A great example of this application is provided by Kodak. Researchers at Kodak used ***FLOW-3D*** to simulate a new printhead design (Fig.1), for a pigment-based ink. CFD simulation allowed them to shave years off the design testing phase and bring a new product to market in a fraction of the time it would normally take.

There are many examples of inkjet type devices that benefit from CFD simulations. For example, Fig.2a shows a bubble generated at the junction of two optical channels. The bubble is intended to act like a switch that changes the direction of a light beam from straight through a junction to right angles into another channel. Researchers were initially not able to make this switch work and were unable to introduce sensing instruments because of its small size. A CFD simulation showed that liquid being evaporated at the bottom of the horizontal channel was condensing on the sides of the vertical channel, causing additional light reflections that prevented a clean switch operation (Fig.2b). Once seeing the problem, a fix was easily introduced that resulted in a smooth change in the light beam direction without having to introduce mechanical means.
heading: Why CFD? > Liquid behavior in inkjet printers

text:
Why CFD? > Large-scale hydropower projects

Another example involves large hydropower projects (dams and power stations), which are difficult to model in laboratory experiments, not only because of the expense, but because it is not possible to scale down the size of large installations without violating some scaling parameters that may change the results in unknown ways. A simple example of this would be a small-scale flume used to study wave propagation through or around various obstacles. At small sizes, surface tension may affect wave heights and wave speeds, while at larger scales surface tension is generally not important. Computational simulations have the flexibility to use any values for physical properties, so are not affected by scaling that would otherwise require a use of materials that may not exist.

The expense issue is, of course, very important. Large hydro projects can cost hundreds of millions of dollars and any errors in design can be catastrophic and are very expensive to correct. Furthermore, large projects involve many diverse types of flow situations that may influence one another.

Consider a hydroelectric power dam. There are intakes that require deflectors for fish or objects that could damage power generators. On the downstream side there is a spillway, the design of which must consider air entrainment which may affect the downstream ecology and cause possible scour damage at the base of the spillway. In case of a large rise in the upstream flow level, allowance must be made for overflow devices to relieve excess water without damaging the dam. Such considerations are why elaborate laboratory models are constructed to model these features. Their construction, however, is time consuming and expensive. And, just as in computational modeling, validation studies are needed to determine their accuracy.

In contrast, computational modeling can easily deal with large scales in which there are diverse flows. When necessary, computational models can be localized to study individual flow features in more detail. This flexibility is a definite advantage over physical models. Setting up a computational model is also much faster and less expensive than constructing a physical model

In the dam example shown in Fig. 3, several alternative designs of a proposed spillway were investigated using CFD simulations that could be quickly and inexpensively set up. Once the best design was selected, a physical model was constructed and used to confirm the CFD results.

An added advantage of using CFD in cases like this is that because it has been validated with the physical model, and while the physical model has been torn down to make room for other projects, future alterations to the dam can now be more quickly and less expensively investigated with confidence using additional computations.
heading: Why CFD? > Large-scale hydropower projects

text:
Why CFD? > Solving novel problems with CFD

The above examples provide reasons for why we use CFD. It must also be mentioned, of course, that CFD does have its limitations. For example, in the large hydro project’s discussion, involving a diverse set of flow issues, it may not be possible to computationally model all the flow features in sufficient detail because of a limitation in computer memory and/or computational cost. Should this be the case then the best solution may be to break up the simulation into manageable parts. The rapid growth in parallel and cloud computing resources is reducing this kind of limitation, but it will continue to exist as long as there are demands for more detail and a reduction in computational cost.

So why CFD? The answer is because it offers solutions to problems that may not be studied as closely, as thoroughly, or indeed in any other way.
heading: Why CFD? > Solving novel problems with CFD

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > What is Cavitation?

Cavitation occurs when the local pressure in a liquid drops below the fluid’s vapor pressure. This can occur due to very low pressure in a flowing fluid or due to a rise in temperature of a liquid that then raises the local vapor pressure. No matter the mechanism this causes the liquid to vaporize and form vapor-filled voids or bubbles. When these bubbles are carried into regions of higher pressure, they collapse violently, generating pressure waves, noise, vibration, and potentially severe surface erosion. Cavitation is a critical concern in hydraulic machinery, valves, pumps, propellers, spillways, and high-pressure casting processes.

The ***FLOW-3D*** product family offers two distinct approaches to cavitation simulation: a physics-based Cavitation Model and a simplified Cavitation Potential Model. Each serves a different purpose, and choosing between them depends on the engineering question you are trying to answer.
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > What is Cavitation?

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Model

The Cavitation Model, available across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family, models the physical process of cavitation directly. When local pressure falls below the vapor pressure threshold, the model drives a phase change from liquid to vapor, forming and tracking vapor regions within the flow field in real time. The reverse process, condensation and bubble collapse, is also captured as pressure recovers.

Two modes are available:

- **Active cavitation** — the model actively enforces the vapor pressure constraint, preventing fluid pressure from falling below the vapor pressure. Vapor voids form and collapse dynamically as the simulation evolves. This model is appropriate when cavitation materially affects the flow behavior, for example when void formation alters velocity fields, or when the fate of the vapor voids is important.
- **Passive cavitation** — the model tracks and transports the presence of cavitation bubbles through the fluid as a dispersed phase but does not form vapor voids. This model is useful when cavitation is secondary effect in the flow, like when only a brief appearance of small bubbles is expected.
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Model

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Model > Example: Butterfly Valve

In this ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulation, water flows through a butterfly valve at conditions where cavitation occurs downstream of the valve body. Using the Active Cavitation Model, vapor voids form and are tracked in real time. The visualization shows the void region alongside the pressure distribution and velocity field with streamlines, capturing not just where cavitation occurs, but how it interacts with the surrounding flow.

**FLOW-3D HYDRO** simulation of a butterfly valve showing cavitation downstream of the valve body (left). Pressure distribution (top right) and velocity magnitude with streamlines (bottom right) show how the vapor void interacts with the surrounding flow.

**Applications include:**

- Hydraulic valves and gates
- Pump inlets and impellers
- Propellers and underwater vehicles
- Orifices and flow control structures
- Spillways
- Pipe systems with rapid pressure transients
- Boiling
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Model > Example: Butterfly Valve

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Potential Model

The Cavitation Potential Model is a diagnostic tool rather than a full multiphase model. Rather than modeling the physical cavitation, it identifies regions in the flow where the local pressure falls below the vapor pressure, flagging zones where cavitation is possible under the simulated conditions.

Because the model does not simulate the phase change itself, it runs with lower computational cost and produces a straightforward spatial map of cavitation risk. This makes it well suited for early-stage design screening, parametric studies across many geometry variants, or applications where the primary question is location of risk rather than quantification of its effects.

Additionally, cavitation can occur in high pressure die casting. The rapid movement of molten alloy through constrictions and curves in the die can result in rapid pressure drops and lead to subsequent cavitation. The resulting vapor bubbles can cause defects in the final casting and cause damage to the die, leading to reduced die life. For these reasons, it is critical to understand where cavitation is likely to occur and its potential severity. Since initiating and visualizing cavitation through physical experimentation is difficult and potentially damaging, it is preferable to simulate the process.
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Potential Model

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Potential Model > Example: HPDC Filling

Cavitation bubbles collapsing on the die surface can create pitting, but simulation of the full cavitation bubble can be simplified to improve performance. **FLOW-3D****CAST**‘s cavitation potential model is a powerful tool for identifying areas on the die where cavitation is likely to occur by tracking the conditions which cause cavitation instead of capturing the cavitation bubbles themselves.

*Side-by-side views of an HPDC die casting simulation showing cavitation potential. Cyan regions indicate where local pressure drops below the vapor pressure threshold, identifying areas at risk for die erosion and casting defects.*
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Cavitation Potential Model > Example: HPDC Filling

text:
Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Choosing Between the Two Models

If cavitation is a central phenomenon in your simulation, one that will influence the behavior of the overall flow, use the full Cavitation Model. If you want to quickly determine where cavitation is likely before committing to a full multiphase run, the Cavitation Potential Model is the right starting point.
heading: Cavitation > Cavitation Model > Choosing Between the Two Models

text:
Air Entrainment Model

Air entrainment occurs when gas bubbles are drawn into a liquid at a free surface through turbulent mixing, impingement, or mechanical agitation. Once entrained, these bubbles are transported by the flow, rise due to buoyancy, and may escape at a free surface or remain trapped within the liquid. The consequences range from beneficial, aerated spillways resist cavitation damage and oxygenated water supports aquatic life; to detrimental, such as gas porosity defects in metal castings or unwanted gas ingestion in fuel systems.

The ***FLOW-3D*** product family’s Air Entrainment Model simulates the entrainment, transport, and escape of undissolved gas bubbles at free surfaces across a wide range of applications and industries. The same underlying model applies whether the fluid is water, molten metal, or liquid fuel; and whether the goal is to maximize aeration or minimize it.
heading: Air Entrainment Model

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Air Entrainment model works in conjunction with the Variable Density and the Drift Flux Models to fully represent the physics of aerated flow. Together, these three models approximate the air entrained at the free surface, the motion of entrained air bubbles through the fluid, and the effect of variable air concentration on the local fluid density. The combined capability includes:

- Local air entrainment rate at the free surface, driven by turbulent kinetic energy exceeding surface stabilizing forces
- Transport of entrained air bubbles through the flow field
- Bubble rise due to buoyancy forces
- Bubble escape when air reaches a free surface
- Bulking — the increase in effective fluid volume due to entrained air — affecting free surface elevation
- Variable density flow fields in aerated regions
- Dynamic average bubble sizes based on breakup and coalesce models
- Full postprocessing output including local and integrated air concentrations, average bubble size, and entrained and escaping air fluxes
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Dissolved Oxygen Model

The Air Entrainment Model is coupled with a dissolved oxygen model that tracks the transfer of oxygen from entrained air bubbles into the surrounding liquid. Three options are available for the definition of the mass transfer coefficient:

- User-defined constant — for cases where the transfer coefficient is known from experiment or empirical data
- Clean bubble assumption (Higbie’s penetration theory) — appropriate for bubbles rising in clean water without surfactant effects
- Dirty bubble assumption — accounts for surfactant effects that reduce oxygen dissolution at the bubble interface

The Dissolved Oxygen Model is particularly valuable for water quality assessments downstream of aeration structures, stilling basins, and diffuser systems.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Dissolved Oxygen Model

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Dissolved Oxygen Model > Example: Plunging Jet

This ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulation of a plunging jet shows both the air entrainment and dissolved oxygen models active simultaneously. The top panel shows dissolved oxygen concentration as it is absorbed and transported through the fluid following air entrainment at the impingement point. The bottom panel shows the corresponding entrained air volume fraction, revealing where air is entrained and how it is carried into the water column.

**FLOW-3D HYDRO** simulation of a plunging jet showing dissolved oxygen concentration (top) and entrained air volume fraction (bottom).
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Dissolved Oxygen Model > Example: Plunging Jet

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Spillway Aeration and Cavitation Protection

At high flow velocities, irregularities on a spillway surface can cause flow separation and local pressure drops that lead to cavitation damage. Entraining air into the flow is an effective mitigation strategy: the presence of air bubbles damps the pressure waves produced by collapsing cavitation voids, significantly reducing surface erosion. ***FLOW-3D*** simulates the turbulent boundary layer growing from the spillway surface, the inception point where air first reaches the free surface, and the subsequent aeration and bulking of the flow downstream.

**FLOW-3D HYDRO** simulation of air entrainment on a self-aerating stepped spillway, showing the 3D free surface (left) and entrained air volume fraction in cross-section (right).
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Spillway Aeration and Cavitation Protection

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Fish Passage and Water Quality

Dissolved oxygen concentration is a key parameter in fish passage design. ***FLOW-3D*** determines the concentrations of air entrained at spillways and weirs and tracks how that oxygen is transported and released downstream. This allows engineers to assess whether dissolved gas levels will remain within safe limits for target fish species, and to identify where supersaturation may become a concern.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Fish Passage and Water Quality

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Municipal Water and Wastewater Systems

Aerated flows are common in municipal infrastructure — drop shafts, sewer overflows, and stormwater tunnels all involve conditions where air is entrained and transported. The model’s buoyancy and bulking outputs accurately represent the variable-density flow conditions in these structures, which is essential for sizing shafts, predicting hydraulic grade lines, and avoiding surcharging.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Municipal Water and Wastewater Systems

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Diffuser and Aeration Systems

Mass sources in ***FLOW-3D*** can introduce air directly into the water column, enabling simulation of bubble diffusers used in wastewater treatment, reservoir destratification, and aquaculture oxygenation systems. The turbulent diffusion of entrained air and dissolved oxygen terms present in the ***FLOW-3D*** product family turbulence models allow for accurate prediction of the very low air concentrations typical of fine-bubble diffuser systems.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Water and Environmental Applications > Diffuser and Aeration Systems

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications

In metal casting, entrained air is a primary source of casting defects. Foundry engineers refer to this phenomenon as air entrapment — air or gas bubbles drawn into the melt during filling that become trapped as the metal solidifies, producing porosity, surface blemishes, and compromised mechanical properties. The ***FLOW-3D*** air entrainment model estimates the amount and location of air entrapment across all casting process types.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications > Gravity and Permanent Mold Casting

In gravity-poured processes, turbulent filling conditions — particularly at the gate, runner transitions, and thin sections — entrain air into the melt. ***FLOW-3D* CAST** tracks the transport of entrained air through the filling cavity and models bubble rise due to buoyancy, including the escape of air at a free surface. This allows engineers to predict where gas porosity is most likely to form and adjust gating geometry or filling speed accordingly.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications > Gravity and Permanent Mold Casting

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications > High Pressure Die Casting

In high pressure die casting (HPDC), the high velocities of molten metal through the runner and gate system create conditions where air entrapment is difficult to avoid entirely. The model estimates entrained and entrapped air concentrations throughout the fill, identifying regions of the cavity where air is most likely to be trapped at the end of fill. This insight informs vent placement, overflow design, and vacuum system requirements.

**FLOW-3D CAST** simulation of entrained and entrapped air during mold filling of an HPDC structural component, showing the geometry (left) and air distribution at end of fill (right).
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Metal Casting Applications > High Pressure Die Casting

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Aerospace and Industrial Applications > Aerospace Fuel Systems

During aircraft maneuvers and spacecraft operations, fuel sloshing can entrain air into the liquid propellant. Air ingestion into fuel delivery systems can disrupt flow to engines or affect the accuracy of fuel quantity measurements. ***FLOW-3D*** simulates fuel sloshing dynamics and the entrainment of air at the liquid surface, helping engineers assess the risk of gas ingestion under defined maneuver profiles and design propellant management devices accordingly.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Aerospace and Industrial Applications > Aerospace Fuel Systems

text:
Air Entrainment Model > Aerospace and Industrial Applications > Air Persistence in Industrial Mixing

In high-shear mixing operations such as food production, cosmetics manufacturing, and chemical processing, rotating impellers and agitators entrain air at the free surface of the product. Unlike water, many mixed products are viscous enough that entrained bubbles rise slowly or not at all, causing air to persist within the product long after it is introduced. Trapped air increases the product volume, reduces bulk density, and can degrade texture, appearance, and shelf life. ***FLOW-3D*** simulates the mixing dynamics along with the entrainment and transport of the air through high-viscosity fluids allowing process engineers to evaluate mixer geometry and operating conditions for their effect on air incorporation and retention.
heading: Air Entrainment Model > Aerospace and Industrial Applications > Air Persistence in Industrial Mixing

text:
General Moving Objects Model

The interaction between moving rigid bodies, or objects, and flowing fluids is a complex physical phenomenon. On one end of the spectrum, the object drives the fluid flow with little effect on the object’s motion, for example the motion of the plunger during filling of a high pressure die casting process. On the other end, the motion of the fluid and the motion of the rigid object are completely coupled, like with floating debris through a culvert. In between, additional forces and torques applied to the moving object can exert considerable influence on the fluid but can be overcome by the motion of the fluid; for example, the thrust and torque applied to a boat moving upstream in a river. Moving objects don’t just interact with the water, but moving objects can collide or come into continuous contact with other moving or stationary objects.

The ***FLOW-3D*** product family offers a diverse set of modeling approaches to simulate the wide range of rigid body motion from fully coupled fluid-object motion to simple rigid body translation. The General Moving Object (GMO) model is one of the most broadly applied capabilities in the product family. Engineers across industries use it to simulate everything from check valves and plungers to wave energy converters and rotating machinery — all without resorting to complex body-fitted meshes or remeshing workflows.
heading: General Moving Objects Model

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Modeling Capabilities

The GMO model supports a wide range of motion and interaction types:

- Up to 500 moving objects per simulation, each with independent motion type
- Six degrees of freedom, rotation about a fixed axis or point, translation in fixed directions, or other more complicated constrained motion patterns
- Fully coupled fluid-object interaction, or user-prescribed motion
- Objects composed of multiple materials, each with defined density
- No restriction on geometry or motion complexity
- Time-dependent forces and torques applied to objects
- Collision dynamics and continuous contact between moving and stationary objects
- Springs, ropes, and mooring lines tethered to objects
- Porosity allowed within objects
- Heat conduction and convection through objects
- Force and torque contributions from hydraulic, gravitational, non-inertial, spring, and user-defined sources
- Full postprocessing output including forces, torques, velocities, and positions
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Prescribed Motion

When the motion of an object is known in advance — such as a gate opening at a defined rate, or a plunger following a specified velocity profile — the GMO model allows that motion to be prescribed directly. The fluid response is then computed as the object moves, without requiring the solver to determine the driving forces dynamically. This is useful for hydraulic control structures, casting shot sleeves, and any application where the motion profile is a design input rather than a simulation output.
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Prescribed Motion

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Prescribed Motion > Example: Tainter Gate Opening

In this ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulation, a tainter gate opens using prescribed rotational velocity about a fixed axis. As the gate lifts, high-velocity flow is released through the opening and over the energy dissipators downstream. The top view shows velocity distribution across the stilling basin; the cross-section below shows the jet profile and hydraulic conditions under the gate.

**FLOW-3D HYDRO** simulation of a tainter gate opening using prescribed rotational motion, showing velocity distribution in plan view (top) and cross-section (bottom).
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Prescribed Motion > Example: Tainter Gate Opening

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion

When an object’s motion is driven by the fluid rather than prescribed, the GMO model solves the coupled system dynamically. Forces and torques acting on the object — from fluid pressure, gravity, springs, or user-defined sources — are computed at each time step and used to update the object’s position and velocity. This enables simulation of floating bodies, fluid-driven mechanisms, wave energy devices, and any system where the interaction between fluid and structure is bidirectional.
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Wave Energy Converter

This ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulation models an oscillating water column wave energy converter using a two-fluid VOF model to simulate air flow through a simple turbine. As waves move the water column inside the device, air is driven back and forth through the turbine, generating kinetic energy. The simulation tracks turbine kinetic energy and air flow rate over time, capturing the oscillatory energy extraction that characterizes this class of device.

**FLOW-3D HYDRO** simulation of a wave energy converter showing the physical device (top left), 2-fluid VOF model cross-section with air velocity (bottom left), and turbine kinetic energy and air flow rate time histories (right).
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Wave Energy Converter

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Rotating Casting Wheel

In this ***FLOW-3D* CAST** simulation, aluminum ingots are produced using a rotating casting wheel. The rotation of the wheel and the translation of the molds are both defined as moving geometry, allowing the complete filling sequence to be modeled as the molds pass under the pouring station. Entrained air concentrations are tracked across successive mold positions, giving engineers insight into where oxide and air inclusions are most likely to occur.

**FLOW-3D CAST** simulation of aluminum ingot production on a rotating casting wheel, showing entrained air distribution across mold positions.
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Rotating Casting Wheel

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Dosing Simulation of HPDC Process

This ***FLOW-3D* CAST** simulation models the process of pouring molten aluminum from a ladle into a shot sleeve. The ladle follows a prescribed pouring motion while the plunger waits at the end of the sleeve. Thermal contours capture the temperature distribution of the melt as it flows through the ladle spout, showing both the thermal loss during dosing and the wave propagation driven by the momentum of the pour. This thermal profile is critical for determining melt conditions in the shot sleeve before the plunger pushes the metal into the die.

**FLOW-3D CAST** dosing simulation showing molten aluminum poured from a ladle into a shot sleeve, colored by temperature. The ladle pouring motion and plunger position are both modeled as GMOs.
heading: General Moving Objects Model > Coupled Fluid-Object Motion > Example: Dosing Simulation of HPDC Process

text:
General Moving Objects Model > Applications

The General Moving Objects model is used across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family for a wide range of engineering problems, including:

- Hydraulic control structures — tainter gates, flap gates, sluice gates
- Check valves and flow-driven valve mechanisms
- Plunger motion in HPDC shot sleeves
- Wave energy converters
- Rotating machinery — casting wheels, mixers, centrifuges
- Automotive gearbox lubrication and fuel sloshing
- Moored and floating bodies in coastal and offshore flows
- Squeeze pins and moving die components in metal casting

text:
Turbulence Models

Turbulence is a physical phenomenon where the inertia of a fluid overcomes the stabilizing effect of viscosity. This causes the various quantities of the flow to vary randomly in time and space over a wide range of scales. These turbulent motions enhance the diffusion of mass, momentum, and other scalars. The irregular nature of turbulent flow requires a statistical description to analyze the quantities of interest. Other than at low Reynolds numbers where viscous effects dominate, turbulence is ubiquitous across all engineering applications.

Various modeling strategies have been developed to account for the effect of turbulence while balancing the computational effort required to include varying levels of physical complexity. One of the most popular modeling approaches is to represent the effect of turbulence as an additional turbulent, or eddy, viscosity that modifies the physical viscosity. The ***FLOW-3D*** product family offers a comprehensive turbulence modeling suite covering fully 3D flows, 2D depth-averaged shallow water flows, and hybrid 3D/2D depth-averaged flows. Various turbulence model options are available, ranging from simple mixing length approaches to robust Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes models to large-eddy simulation, giving engineers the flexibility to match model complexity to the demands of their application.
heading: Turbulence Models

text:
Turbulence Models > Example: Von Kármán Vortex Street

The simulation below illustrates one of LES’s key strengths: the ability to resolve coherent turbulent structures in detail. A bluff body placed in a flow generates a von Kármán vortex street, a classic pattern of alternating vortices shed from either side of the object. The Q-criterion isosurfaces, colored by velocity magnitude, reveal the three-dimensional structure of these vortices as they form, stretch, and dissipate downstream. A RANS model is only capable of capturing the time-dependent mean behavior of the shedding vortices; LES captures their full transient behavior.
heading: Turbulence Models > Example: Von Kármán Vortex Street

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models

Turbulence models in 3D directly model the effect of the unresolved turbulent fluctuations. For RANS, that is the effect of turbulence on the mean flow. For LES, that is the effect on the resolved transient fluctuating flow.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Prandtl Mixing Length Model

One of the earliest turbulence models, the Prandtl mixing length approach estimates turbulent effects by assuming the turbulent viscosity is proportional to a constant user-specified length scale. It remains useful for simple academic cases and benchmarking but is no longer widely applied to complex industrial flows.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Prandtl Mixing Length Model

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > One-Equation Model

The one-equation model solves a transport equation for the turbulent kinetic energy k but requires the specification of a constant turbulent mixing length at all locations to calculate the turbulent viscosity. Because this length scale is rarely known in advance for complex geometries, this model is generally limited to simple flows.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > One-Equation Model

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Standard k-epsilon Model

The standard k-epsilon model (Harlow & Nakayama, 1967) solves transport equations for both turbulent kinetic energy k and turbulent dissipation rate epsilon, computing the mixing length and thus the turbulent viscosity dynamically. It is an industry standard with a broad validation base and performs well across a wide range of flows (Rodi, 1980).
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Standard k-epsilon Model

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > RNG k-epsilon Model

The Renormalized Group (RNG) k-epsilon model (Yakhot & Orszag, 1986; Yakhot & Smith, 1992) is a more robust extension of the standard k-epsilon approach. It provides better performance in transitionally turbulent flows, curving flows, wall heat transfer, and mass transfer, and is the recommended starting point for most industrial problems.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > RNG k-epsilon Model

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > k-omega Model

The k-omega model (Wilcox, 1988, 1998, 2008) replaces the dissipation rate with omega (epsilon/k), offering improved accuracy for free shear flows with streamwise pressure gradients such as spreading jets, wakes, and plumes.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > k-omega Model

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Large Eddy Simulation (LES)

Rather than modeling the effect of turbulence statistically, LES resolves most turbulent fluctuations directly and models the unresolved turbulence using an additional subgrid-scale (SGS) viscosity term. Just like with the turbulent viscosity of the RANS models, the SGS viscosity modifies the physical viscosity. It requires significantly finer mesh resolution than RANS models and provides detailed transient statistics of the flow field. Time-averaging LES output produces results very similar to RANS, as shown in the fish passage comparison below.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Large Eddy Simulation (LES)

text:
Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Example: Turbulence Model Comparison of a Fish Passage

The three simulations below use the same fish passage geometry to compare turbulence models in practice. The first video shows the LES model with instantaneous velocity fluctuations visible. The second shows the time-averaged result from the same LES simulation. The third uses the RNG k-epsilon model. The time-averaged LES and RNG k-epsilon results are closely comparable, demonstrating that RANS models can provide an efficient and accurate alternative to LES for time-averaged quantities in certain types of problems.
heading: Turbulence Models > 3D Turbulence Models > Example: Turbulence Model Comparison of a Fish Passage

text:
Turbulence Models > Wall Function

Viscous boundary layers that develop along solid surfaces influence the bulk turbulent flow. Since these boundary layers can be extremely thin, it can be computationally expensive to resolve them for general engineering applications. An alternative approach is to model the effect of the unresolved portion of the boundary layer on the rest of the resolved flow using a wall function. Each turbulence model in the ***FLOW-3D*** product family employs a wall function based on the logarithmic law of the wall at any smooth or rough solid surface.
heading: Turbulence Models > Wall Function

text:
Turbulence Models > Dynamic Maximum Mixing Length

For the two-equation RANS turbulence models, the local bounds of the turbulent length and time scales can be computed dynamically based on limiters from the Kolmogorov scales on the lower bound and integral scales on the upper bound. These dynamic limiters allow for the modeling of a wider range of flows without requiring the specification of a constant maximum turbulent length scale. This is particularly valuable for applications such as contact tanks and water treatment systems where complex flow conditions span a broad range of turbulent states.
heading: Turbulence Models > Dynamic Maximum Mixing Length

text:
Turbulence Models > Shallow Water Turbulence Models

For 2D depth-averaged and shallow water regions of hybrid 3D/2D flows, the effect of unresolved turbulent fluctuations is accounted for using a scalar model for turbulent viscosity. The effect of dispersion of the velocity in the vertical direction can also be accounted for in some of the models. See the Shallow Water Model capabilities page for more information about the specific shallow water turbulence models available within *FLOW-3D***HYDRO**.
heading: Turbulence Models > Shallow Water Turbulence Models

Turbulence models in the ***FLOW-3D*** product family are applied across a wide range of industries and flow types, including:

- Hydraulic infrastructure such as spillways, fish passages, contact tanks, and pump stations

text:
FAVOR vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates

The simplicity of the fractional area/volume FAVOR™ method for modeling complex geometric regions is very attractive. But, does its accuracy compete with deformed grids like finite-element or body-fitted coordinate methods? A comparison between these methods shows that there are only small differences between the inherent capabilities of the two approaches.

In the absence of solid boundaries there is little fundamental difference between grids of differently shaped control volumes. Some methods require users to store more information (e.g., node locations and various geometric factors) and some exhibit differing levels of accuracy depending on the amount of element distortion. In all cases, however, the underlying idea is a discrete approximation in which fluid forces and fluxes are computed for each element in the grid.

It is the issue of obstacle boundaries that is most often raised as an advantage of deformable grids because they can be constructed to fit the geometry. Two consequences come with this flexibility. One consequence is that these grids must be unstructured for general use. This is because structured grids can only undergo limited distortion before elements are turned inside out. The other consequence is that the distortion of an element makes it more difficult to construct accurate numerical approximations.
heading: FAVOR vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates

text:
FAVOR vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > Structured FAVOR™ Grids vs. Unstructured Grids

The FAVOR™ concept can be used in connection with any type of grid including grids consisting of rectangular or distorted elements and whether the grid is structured or unstructured. Structured grids are best because they are easy to generate and the indices for neighboring elements are known. Rectangular grid elements make it easy to compute the fractional areas and volumes of elements used by the FAVOR™ method.

The ease with which structured, rectangular grids can be generated makes this an obvious choice for the FAVOR™ method. However, the specification of open and closed grid regions implicit in the FAVOR™ method introduces a type of unstructured computing environment, because only those elements having a finite amount of open volume are actually computed. This results in a computation that is analogous to an unstructured grid computation.

The analogy with a true unstructured grid is not perfect. For example, the FAVOR™ method requires storage for all elements whether they are blocked or not, while unstructured grids require storage of neighbor lists. Storing all elements is the price paid for automatically knowing which elements are neighbors. Of course, if heat conduction is to be computed in the solid regions surrounding a fluid, then blocked elements must be kept anyway.

One disadvantage associated with rectangular, structured grids is that they cannot be distorted to increase resolution in a localized region. Grid lines can be constructed closer together in a particular region for increased resolution, but these grid lines then extend across the entire grid. As a result, the number of elements in a grid may become large. Offsetting this disadvantage is the simplicity of grid generation. There is also the possibility of introducing multiple grid blocks joined at their boundaries to provide increased local resolution without a large increase in the number of grid cells.

The FAVOR™ method is seen to have properties analogous to unstructured grids but without the overhead associated with the construction of unstructured body-fitted or finite-element grids. Since grid generation often requires a major investment of time and effort, the elimination of this task makes FAVOR™ a very desirable alternative.
heading: FAVOR vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > Structured FAVOR™ Grids vs. Unstructured Grids

text:
FAVOR vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ vs. Body-Fitted Coordinates > FAVOR™ Elements vs. Body-Fitted Coordinate Elements

A second issue with deformed grids is that their deformation can be used to fit a bounding solid surface. This is accomplished by moving the nodes of elements closest to the surface onto the surface. In contrast, in the FAVOR™ method a surface is allowed to cut through an element and its location is recorded not by moving the edges of the element but in terms of the fractional face areas and fractional volume of the element that are not covered by the solid.

What we wish to show is that this fractional area/volume technique for defining solid boundaries has the same consequences for numerical approximation as does a deformed (i.e., body-fitted coordinates) grid technique.

The most important point to recognize about the FAVOR™ method is that approximations of fluid-dynamic quantities are restricted to the open regions of elements. This restriction introduces fractional areas and volumes of elements as factors directly into the discrete approximations. For example, the flux of a quantity from one element to another has the fractional area of the fluxing boundary that is open to flow as a multiplier.

In this way FAVOR™ and body-fitted coordinates both compute fluxes across the faces of elements that employ the same areas. In FAVOR™ the areas are stored as fractions of the original element face areas. In a BFC method the areas are computed from the coordinates of the nodes defining the faces, and often times they are also stored so they don’t have to be recomputed.

When constructing difference approximations in a grid of non-uniform elements it is necessary to know the effective element widths in different directions. A simple example is given in Fig. 1, which shows an element with a solid boundary. In this case the solid boundary is parallel with the vertical sides of the element. For a deformed element, Fig. 1b, the width of the cell would be h and this width would be used for computing differences in the horizontal direction.

In FAVOR™ the width of the open portion of the cell is equal to the product of the open volume fraction and the original cell width. It is this product that is used in FAVOR™ for difference approximations in the horizontal direction and it is the same as the width of the deformed cell, h.

When differences are computed in a vertical direction, for example, across the top of the element (i.e., parallel to the solid boundary in Fig. 1) the FAVOR™ method approximation involves a ratio of the fractional area at the top divided by the fractional volume. This ratio has a value of unity because the solid boundary blocks the same fraction of area horizontally as it does volume, which again makes the approximation similar to that of a BFC cell. Thus, there is no difference between the effective cell widths used in making difference approximations in FAVOR™ and body-fitted coordinate cells.

If the solid surface is slanted as shown in Fig. 2, then the top and bottom face areas are different but are still known quantities in either case. Further, the average horizontal width of the open portion of the cell (h) is still the same because the volume fraction does not change when the solid surface is rotated about a midpoint within the cell (see dashed line). Here again there is little to distinguish between a FAVOR™ and a body-fitted coordinate cell.

It is well known that body-fitted coordinate grids can be difficult to construct, and there has been effort devoted to the development of automatic grid generators. It is also well known that even with the best of grid generators it still takes a significant amount of time to establish a workable well-behaved grid.

The simple rectangular construction of FAVOR™ grids makes them extremely easy to generate. Fractional areas and fractional volumes must be computed to define obstacles placed within a grid, but theses computations are well defined and easy to automate using simple algorithms.

Numerical accuracy is not sacrificed when selecting FAVOR™ over a body-fitted coordinate gridding method. The two approaches simply represent different ways to approximate bounding surfaces.

Finally, the numerical advantages inherent in the structured, smoothly varying, strictly orthogonal grids used by the FAVOR™ method should not be overlooked. These advantages, as well as the ability to automatically represent porous media (i.e., another example of a fractional area/volume region) are additional reasons why the FAVOR™ method was selected as the basis of ***FLOW-3D***.

text:
Cast Iron Model

Cast iron solidification is fundamentally different from most other casting alloys. While aluminum and steel contract during solidification, cast iron undergoes a complex interplay of shrinkage and expansion driven by the formation of different microstructural phases. Getting this balance right is critical: too much shrinkage leads to porosity, while unconstrained expansion can cause mold distortion or surface defects.

The Cast Iron Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** describes the solidification of hypo- and hyper-eutectic iron-carbon-silicon alloys, predicting the formation of graphite, austenite, and carbide phases during the eutectic reaction. By coupling microstructure evolution with volumetric changes and heat release, the model gives foundry engineers accurate predictions of shrinkage, expansion, and porosity risk across the full range of gray and ductile iron alloys.
heading: Cast Iron Model

text:
Cast Iron Model > How the Model Works

The Cast Iron Model computes the solidification path from a realistic iron-carbon phase diagram using the initial carbon and silicon composition of the melt. As the metal cools through the eutectic region, the model determines the local formation rates of graphite, austenite, and carbide at each point in the casting. The latent heat release is computed as a direct function of temperature along this freezing path, rather than using a simple fixed latent heat value.

The key to accurate cast iron simulation is the chilling susceptibility criterion, which controls how much carbide forms relative to graphite at each location. In well-inoculated gray iron, graphite dominates and the iron expands during eutectic solidification. Near mold walls and in thin sections where cooling is rapid, the chilling tendency increases and carbide formation dominates, producing local shrinkage and harder white iron zones. The model captures this spatial variation, enabling prediction of chill zones without requiring separate analysis. The actual value of the chilling susceptibility criterion must be determined experimentally, for example, from an ASTM chill-wedge test.

The Cast Iron Model works in conjunction with the Simple Shrinkage Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST**, coupling the density changes from phase formation directly to porosity and shrinkage predictions. The model can also be used together with the general solidification model with flow. However, volume changes associated with the formation of different phases are only coupled to the simple shrinkage model that does not include flow.
heading: Cast Iron Model > How the Model Works

text:
Cast Iron Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Cast Iron Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** predicts:

- Graphite, austenite, and carbide phase fractions throughout the casting as solidification progresses
- Local chilling tendency based on eutectic front velocity, enabling spatial prediction of white iron zones near mold walls and in thin sections
- Latent heat release as a function of the realistic iron freezing path, derived from carbon and silicon composition
- Liquid shrinkage during cooling from pouring temperature to the start of solidification
- Coupling with the Simple Porosity Model to predict porosity risk from net volumetric changes
- Sensitivity to inoculation state through the chilling susceptibility parameter, which can be calibrated from standard chill wedge tests
heading: Cast Iron Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Cast Iron Model > Applications

The Cast Iron Model is used in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** for:

- Predicting shrinkage porosity in gray and ductile iron castings based on alloy composition and cooling conditions
- Identifying chill zones in iron castings and evaluating the effect of inoculation on microstructure
- Optimizing riser design for iron castings, where the expansion/shrinkage balance varies across the casting
- Evaluating the effect of pouring temperature on graphite and carbide formation
- Supporting alloy composition selection to achieve the desired balance of graphite and carbide
- Assessing the risk of hard spots and machinability issues from local carbide formation
heading: Cast Iron Model > Applications

text:
Modeling Capabilities

At the core of the ***FLOW-3D*** product family is **TruVOF**, the proprietary volume-of-fluid algorithm that has defined the standard for free surface flow simulation for more than four decades. Built on this foundation, the product family includes a comprehensive set of physics models covering multiphase and multicomponent flows, heat transfer, turbulence, fluid-structure interaction, particle dynamics, and a range of specialized capabilities including the Immersed Boundary Method and Detailed Cutcell Representation for improved near-wall accuracy. Individual model availability varies by product. These models can be activated in combination within a single simulation to address the full complexity of real engineering problems.

This is a ***FLOW-3D* AM** simulation of laser wire-based directed energy deposition with IN718. In this example, you can see the complex interplay of heat transfer, surface tension, viscosity, and phase change for consistent bead deposition. ***FLOW-3D* AM** is useful for understanding the processing windows for wire-based DED and allows for optimization studies to find the best processing parameters such as wire feed rate and diameter for a build.

Simulation of laser powder bed fusion with IN718 powder. Analysis provides detail on lack of fusion porosity for 10 layers including thermal gradients and cooling rates for microstructure prediction, and surface topology for predicting surface roughness.

In this simulation, we look at fluid impact on a powder bed. The material properties of the fluid and the process parameters such as powder size distribution and droplet velocities influence the spreading, coalescence and penetration of the fluid into the powder bed. Capillary forces help the fluid to penetrate further into the powder bed. The mass-averaged kinetic energy plot shows that the fluid eventually reaches steady state indicating the depth of penetration and seepage into the medium.

Porosity is a critical defect in aluminum laser welding that can compromise joint strength and electrical conductivity. This ***FLOW-3D* WELD** simulation demonstrates laser welding of aluminum with visualization of porosity evolution throughout the welding process. CFD modeling helps engineers understand how gas bubbles form, grow, and become trapped during solidification, enabling optimization of process parameters to minimize porosity in aluminum welds.

Lap weld quality depends on multiple factors including thermal management, penetration depth, and defect formation throughout the welding process. This ***FLOW-3D* WELD** simulation demonstrates laser lap welding with visualization of thermal evolution, porosity formation, bead dimensions, and melt volume. CFD modeling helps engineers assess joint quality and optimize process parameters to achieve desired weld characteristics while minimizing defects in lap joint configurations.

Pulsed laser welding creates distinct weld bead patterns that require careful control of process parameters to achieve consistent joint quality. This ***FLOW-3D* WELD** simulation demonstrates pulsed laser welding of a T-joint, capturing the characteristic stacked dime effect created by individual laser pulses. CFD modeling helps engineers optimize energy density and pulse duration for improved fusion, reduced defects, and better penetration depth in T-joint configurations.

In combination with the realistic flow simulation, ***FLOW-3D* CAST** is able to accurately represent the flows and turbulence as well as possible oxide or air inclusions in the melt. This ***FLOW-3D*** simulation of a forward roll coating process captures a ribbing defect due to a high capillary number. The model incorporates the effects of surface tension and viscosity as the backing rollers draw the fluid through a 400 micron nip. The simulation is based on research described in the paper ‘Ribbing instability in rigid and deformable forward roll coating flows’ presented in the Korea-Australia Rheology Journal Vol. 22. The accurate prediction of the onset of ribbing allows for researchers to identify optimal process parameters to avoid defects.

This simulation shows a single-layer curtain coating process. ***FLOW-3D*** can be used to investigate the stability of the coating process under different process parameters such as flow rate, flow width, and substrate speed, as well as changes to the liquid’s physical properties like viscosity, surface tension, and adhesion force.

In this simulation of a multi-layer slide curtain coating process, three layers of liquid are ejected from a slot die and allowed to flow under gravity to a substrate. ***FLOW-3D*** can be used to investigate the stability of curtain coating processes under different process parameters such as flow rate, flow width, and substrate speed, as well as changes to the liquid’s physical properties like viscosity, surface tension, and adhesion force.

In this hydrodynamic microfluidic separation simulation, you can see particle sorting based on varying diameters. The technique works on the principle that a particle will follow a streamline. Particles with the smallest diameter (blue) get easily carried towards the top of the constriction and hence at the divergence follow the streamlines that diverge upwards. Particles with the largest diameter (green) stay their course and move towards the bottom of the constriction. Upon exiting the constriction, these particles follow the streamlines that diverge downwards.

Electrowetting is a technique used to change the apparent contact angle of a dielectric fluid under the influence of electric potential. In this example, the fluid is originally hydrophobic and beads on the surface. However, when a 50V potential difference is applied, the fluid is forced to wet the surface becoming hydrophilic.

Joule heating occurs when an electric current passes through a conducting material, such as a fluid. At a microscopic level, Joule heating is caused by interactions between moving charged particles. Additionally, if the fluid is dielectric, polarization will happen in the presence of an electric field causing fluid flow. ***FLOW-3D*** can capture all such effects, which is demonstrated by the simulation, which highlights the software‘s ability to accurately capture electro-kinetics physics.

Metal Casting Models

At the foundation of **FLOW-3D****CAST** is the accuracy of the filling simulation. **FLOW-3D****CAST** is built on the same solver engine that powers the ***FLOW-3D*** product family, with a specialized interface and physics models designed specifically for metal casting. The **TruVOF** free surface tracking algorithm resolves the metal front with a precision that directly improves the quality of every subsequent result: where air is entrapped during filling determines where gas porosity appears; where the metal arrives cold determines where cold shuts form; how heat is distributed at end of fill sets the initial conditions for solidification. Heat transfer between the metal, die, and cooling system is solved continuously throughout filling and solidification, making it central to every casting simulation. These physics models work together within a single simulation environment, so the interactions between filling conditions and downstream outcomes are captured without separate software or manual data transfer.

Water & Environmental Models

Many civil hydraulic and environmental engineering applications involve complex, transient free surface flows where three-dimensional CFD is needed to understand the physics of the problem in order to provide actionable information to make engineering decisions. Scour around a bridge pier, wave loading on a coastal structure, aerated flow down a spillway, and tailings runout following a dam failure all include additional multi-physics processes that add complexity to the free surface flow being studied.

***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** is built on the same solver engine that powers the ***FLOW-3D*** product family, with a set of physics models designed specifically for water resources and environmental engineering. Those models account for the physical processes that matter in practice. The result is a tool that moves seamlessly between municipal hydraulics, river engineering, dam safety, ports and coastal infrastructure, and mine waste management.
heading: Water & Environmental Models
