text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model

Flow through porous materials governs some of the most important processes in engineering and the natural sciences. Groundwater moves through aquifers and embankments. Resins infiltrate fiber preforms in composite manufacturing. Fuel cells transport gases through porous electrodes. Filtration systems separate particles from fluids. Geological formations store and transmit oil, gas, and water over vast distances. In all of these systems, the resistance of the porous structure to flow, the capillary forces at the fluid-solid interface, and the degree of saturation all interact to determine how the fluid moves.

The Porous Media Model is available across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family and simulates both saturated and unsaturated flows within porous structures, fully coupled to the free surface flow solver. Porosity, permeability, and wettability can be specified independently for each component in the model, giving engineers precise control over how different regions of the domain resist and transmit flow. Permeability can be isotropic or anisotropic, and several drag law formulations are available to cover the full range of flow regimes from slow Darcian creep to higher velocity inertial flow.

*A droplet source moves in a circular pattern while ejecting droplets downward into a porous medium, creating a ring-shaped deposition pattern.*
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media

Saturated flow occurs when the pores of the material are fully occupied by liquid, with a relatively sharp interface between the saturated and unsaturated zones. This is the relevant regime for groundwater flow, flow through filter media, and most pressure-driven infiltration applications. The ***FLOW-3D***product family provides two drag law formulations for saturated porous flow: Darcian Drag and Forcheimer Drag.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media > Darcian Drag

The resistance to flow is modeled using Darcy’s Law in which the flow rate through a porous medium is proportional to the applied pressure gradient, with the proportionality determined by the permeability of the material. This relationship holds in the low-velocity regime where viscous forces dominate and inertia is negligible.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media > Darcian Drag

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media > Forchheimer Drag

At higher flow velocities, inertial effects become significant and the linear Darcy relationship underestimates the true pressure drop. The Forchheimer model extends Darcy’s Law by adding a quadratic drag term that accounts for inertial losses at the pore scale.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Saturated Porous Media > Forchheimer Drag

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Capillary Pressure in Saturated Media

When a wetting fluid is in contact with a porous material, surface tension at the fluid-gas interface inside the pores generates a capillary pressure that drives absorption. For saturated porous media, this capillary pressure is a fixed value determined by the average pore diameter, the surface tension of the fluid, and the contact angle of the fluid on the solid. A positive capillary pressure drives absorption into a wetting material; a negative capillary pressure (non-wetting) means that external pressure must be applied to force the fluid into the pores.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Capillary Pressure in Saturated Media

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Unsaturated Porous Media

Unsaturated flow occurs when both liquid and gas are present within the pore space, with a gradual transition between the fully saturated and dry zones. There is no fixed capillary pressure; instead, capillary pressure varies continuously with local saturation. This regime describes wicking, drainage, and moisture transport in porous materials where the saturation history matters.

***FLOW-3D*** uses the Volume of Fluid method to track the local fluid fraction throughout the porous domain, which acts as the saturation variable. Both the drag coefficient and the capillary pressure are functions of the local saturation, and both filling and draining curves can be specified independently to capture the hysteresis that is characteristic of real porous materials.

Three unsaturated drag models are available:

- Power law model: drag is related to saturation through a power-law relationship, the simplest and most commonly used approach
- Exponential model: drag is related to saturation through an exponential relationship, more physically descriptive than the power law model
- Mualem’s drag model for relative permeability: drag is related to the saturation through an additional relationship based on a relative permeability, strong experimental basis

Two unsaturated capillary pressure models are available:

- Simplified model: assumes a linear scanning curve between wetting and draining capillary pressure versus local saturation curves
- Van Genuchten model: a smooth, differentiable saturation-permeability relationship that provides a better fit to many real soil types, particularly for fine-grained materials
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Unsaturated Porous Media

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Anisotropic Permeability

In many real porous materials, flow resistance is not the same in all directions. Layered sediments, fiber-reinforced composites, and directionally compacted filter media all exhibit different permeabilities depending on the flow direction. The ***FLOW-3D*** product family supports fully anisotropic permeability specification, where independent permeability values can be assigned for each of the three coordinate directions. This allows accurate representation of materials such as carbon fiber preforms, where permeability along the fiber direction can be orders of magnitude higher than the transverse permeability.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Anisotropic Permeability

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Porous Baffle Plates

In addition to volumetric porous media regions, the ***FLOW-3D*** product family supports thin porous baffles: surfaces that impose a flow resistance without occupying a finite volume in the mesh. Porous baffles are useful for modeling perforated plates, screen meshes, filter membranes, and other thin resistive elements where the physical thickness is much smaller than the mesh cell size. The pressure drop across a baffle is defined by linear and quadratic resistance coefficients, consistent with the Forchheimer formulation for volumetric porous media.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Porous Baffle Plates

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Moisture Drying Model

Building on the unsaturated porous media framework, the Moisture Drying Model simulates the evaporation of moisture from porous materials as heat is applied. This is relevant to drying processes in food manufacturing, pharmaceutical production, construction materials, and any application where the thermal and moisture transport in a porous solid are coupled. The model tracks the distribution of moisture within the porous component and computes the evaporation rate as a function of local temperature and saturation.
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Moisture Drying Model

text:
Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Applications

The Porous Media Model is used across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family for:

- Resin transfer molding and liquid composite molding: tracking resin infiltration through fiber preforms
- Absorbent product design: fluid absorption and wicking through nonwoven fabrics and superabsorbent materials, used in hygiene and medical product development
- Fuel cell modeling: gas transport through porous electrodes and diffusion layers
- Filter and membrane performance analysis: pressure drop and flow distribution in filtration equipment
- Oil and gas reservoir simulation: multiphase flow through porous rock formations
- Soil moisture transport and irrigation system design
- Inkjet and coating processes: fluid absorption into paper, fabric, and other porous substrates
- Heat exchanger design with porous inserts for flow distribution and heat transfer enhancement
- Drying processes in food, pharmaceutical, and construction material manufacturing
- Packed bed reactor design and flow distribution analysis
heading: Porous Media > Porous Media Model > Applications

text:
Cooling Channels

In die casting and permanent mold casting, cooling channels are drilled or cast into the die to extract heat from the mold and control the solidification of the casting. Their design has a direct impact on cycle time, die life, and casting quality. Too little cooling leads to hot spots, shrinkage porosity, and premature die failure. Too much or poorly placed cooling can cause premature solidification, cold shuts, and thermal fatigue cracking in the die.

The Cooling Channels model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** simulates the thermal interaction between cooling circuits and the die across the full casting cycle, from filling and solidification through die opening, spray cooling, and the next fill. Engineers can evaluate channel placement, temperature setpoints, flow activation timing, and thermocouple control strategies to optimize thermal management before any tooling is cut.
heading: Cooling Channels

text:
Cooling Channels > Modeling Capabilities

The Cooling Channels model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** supports:

- Time-dependent coolant temperature and heat transfer coefficients for each channel
- Independent activation schedules per channel, allowing selective cooling and heating at different stages of the cycle
- Thermocouple-controlled activation, where channels switch on or off based on measured wall or metal temperature at a user-defined probe location
- Both cooling mode and heating mode thermocouple control, supporting die preheating as well as active cooling
- Multiple channels with identical or different properties, each defined as separate geometry
- Full integration with thermal die cycling simulations for quasi-steady die temperature analysis over multiple cycles
- Integration with the Solidification Model and Microporosity Formation Model to assess the effect of cooling strategy on casting quality
- Visual cooling channel timeline showing when each channel is active alongside other process timings, added in 2024R1 to simplify setup and reduce input errors
- Moving components, such as sliders and plungers with cooling channels moves with them during motion.
heading: Cooling Channels > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Cooling Channels > How the Model Works

Rather than simulating the fluid flow inside each cooling channel, **FLOW-3D****CAST** models the cooling effect using an effective heat transfer coefficient and coolant temperature assigned to the channel geometry. This approach is computationally efficient and accurate for the thermal management questions that matter most in casting process design. In practice, this means engineers can model complex multi-channel cooling systems, including conformal and conventional drilled circuits, without the added cost of full internal flow simulation, while still accurately capturing their effect on die temperature and casting solidification.

Each cooling channel can have its own temperature, heat transfer coefficient, and activation schedule, allowing complex real-world cooling systems to be represented accurately. Channels can be activated and deactivated at specified times during the cycle, or controlled automatically by thermocouples that monitor wall or metal temperature at defined probe locations in the die.

*Shrinkage void regions with cooling channels (left) and without cooling channels (right), showing how thermal management directly affects shrinkage location and volume.*
heading: Cooling Channels > How the Model Works

text:
Cooling Channels > Thermal Die Cycling

Cooling channel design is most meaningful when evaluated over many casting cycles, not just a single fill. ***FLOW-3D* CAST**’s Thermal Die Cycling capability simulates the die temperature over repeated cycles until a quasi-steady state is reached, with no fluid flow modeled during the thermal-only stages. Each cycle can be divided into up to five stages representing filling, metal cooling, casting removal, die preparation (spray cooling and cleaning), and die closed time before the next fill.

This allows engineers to determine whether the cooling system maintains the die within the desired temperature window cycle after cycle, identify hot spots that accumulate heat over multiple cycles, and evaluate the trade-off between cycle time and die temperature stability.

The Thermal Die Cycling model was redesigned with a simpler, more intuitive setup process that aligns with standard process sheets used in high pressure die casting. The TDC sequence now starts at the beginning of the filling stage, and treatment schedules can be defined on a part-by-part basis. Cooling channels and heating elements move with sliders, and the full sequence of stages, schedules, movements, treatments, and assembly steps is shown in a single overview dialog.
heading: Cooling Channels > Thermal Die Cycling

text:
Cooling Channels > Applications

The Cooling Channels model is used across die casting and permanent mold casting applications to:

- Optimize cooling channel placement to reduce cycle time without compromising casting quality
- Identify and eliminate hot spots that cause shrinkage porosity or premature die failure
- Design thermocouple control strategies for consistent die temperature across production runs
- Evaluate the effect of coolant temperature and flow rate changes on die thermal balance
- Assess die life by predicting thermal fatigue risk from temperature gradients in the die
- Validate cooling system designs before committing to tooling, reducing costly design iterations
- Support die design for high-volume HPDC structural components where thermal management is critical
heading: Cooling Channels > Applications

text:
Active Simulation Control

**products that enables event-driven, closed-loop simulation logic without stopping or restarting the solver. Engineers use Active Simulation Control to replicate real-world process controls inside the simulation: adaptive boundary conditions, dynamic moving object velocities, automated valve sequencing, and conditional simulation termination, all driven by monitored flow quantities in real time. Most engineering processes are dynamic than static. A plunger accelerates as metal reaches the gates. A pressurization valve opens when ullage pressure drops below a threshold. A mixer starts rotating when the fill level reaches a target height. Capturing these conditional, event-driven behaviors requires more than setting initial conditions and letting the solver run. Active Simulation Control in the**

*FLOW-3D*
**product family allows engineers to define logical triggers that monitor simulated flow conditions in real time and respond by modifying simulation parameters, without stopping or restarting the run. The result is a simulation that behaves like a closed-loop control system, adapting dynamically to what is happening in the flow.**

*FLOW-3D*
heading: Active Simulation Control

text:
Active Simulation Control > Active Simulation Control Highlights

- Defines logical triggers (conditions) that monitor flow quantities such as pressure, velocity, temperature, and fluid depth, then initiate actions when thresholds are met
- Control moving objects, boundary conditions, valves, squeeze pins, heat sources, droplet sources, and output frequency, all within a single uninterrupted simulation run
- Supports up to 10 conditions per event with AND/OR logic; global conditions can be shared across multiple events
- Applies across industries including metal casting, additive manufacturing, water and environmental engineering, and aerospace
heading: Active Simulation Control > Active Simulation Control Highlights

text:
Active Simulation Control > How It Works

Active Simulation Control is built around two concepts: conditions and actions, grouped into events.
heading: Active Simulation Control > How It Works

text:
Active Simulation Control > How It Works > Conditions

Conditions monitor quantities from history probes, sampling volumes, flux surfaces, or general history outputs and evaluate whether a logical threshold has been crossed. For example: fluid depth at a probe exceeds 3.25 m, pressure at a probe drops below 1 atmosphere, or average velocity on a flux plane rises above a target value. Allowing conditions based on flow information from sampling volumes and flux surfaces, in addition to point probes, provides more robust control based on spatially averaged quantities rather than single-point measurements; for example, triggering fast shot when the average metal velocity across a flux plane at the gates exceeds a threshold, rather than relying on a single probe that could be affected by local flow variability. Up to 10 conditions can be grouped into a single event, with AND or OR logic controlling whether all conditions or any condition must be met to trigger the event.
heading: Active Simulation Control > How It Works > Conditions

text:
Active Simulation Control > How It Works > Actions

Actions define what changes when an event fires. An action can modify virtually any controllable parameter in the simulation: the velocity of a moving object, the flow rate at a boundary, the output frequency, the state of a valve or vent, or the activation of a squeeze pin. Multiple actions can be assigned to a single event, and multiple events can be defined for a single object.

Conditions can be defined locally for each event, or as global conditions that are shared across multiple events, simplifying setup in complex multi-stage simulations.
heading: Active Simulation Control > How It Works > Actions

text:
Active Simulation Control > What Active Simulation Control Can Control

Active Simulation Control events can be applied to:

- General Moving Objects: translational and angular velocity
- Boundary conditions: pressure, temperature, velocity, volume flow rate, thermal power, density, and scalar concentrations
- Mass and mass/momentum sources: flow rate, velocity, temperature, and scalar concentrations
- Droplet sources: velocity, temperature, pressure, density, radius, and emission interval
- Heat sources and sinks at geometry components
- Cooling channels: on/off control
- Phantom components (solidified fluid velocity): velocity control for continuous casting and additive manufacturing applications
- Squeeze pins: activation based on fluid temperature or solid fraction
- Valves and vents: on/off status, external pressure, and temperature
- Output control: restart, history, and selected data output intervals
- Simulation termination: end a run when a condition is met rather than at a fixed time
heading: Active Simulation Control > What Active Simulation Control Can Control

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > High Pressure Die Casting

In high pressure die casting (HPDC), the injection plunger must transition from slow shot to fast shot at precisely the right moment. Too early and air is entrained in the shot sleeve; too late and the metal front arrives cold. Active Simulation Control can monitor when metal reaches the gates using flux surfaces or sampling volumes and trigger the plunger velocity change automatically. Similarly, deceleration at end of fill to prevent impact pressure spikes can be triggered by metal reaching a specified position in the overflow system.

The PQ2 analysis model can also be applied to control velocity boundary conditions and mass inputs, making it possible to approximate the shot sleeve and plunger with simplified boundary conditions while still tracking whether the HPDC machine is operating within its performance envelope. This significantly reduces simulation time for large and complex castings, including giga-castings, while maintaining filling accuracy.
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > High Pressure Die Casting

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Gravity and Tilt Pour Casting

Gravity casting often uses a pouring basin to maintain a constant pressure head over the sprue. Active Simulation Control can monitor the fluid height in the basin and control the pour rate to keep it at a target level, preventing premature sprue exposure or overflow.
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Gravity and Tilt Pour Casting

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Continuous Casting

In continuous casting, Active Simulation Control manages the withdrawal velocity of the solidifying billet or slab, adjusting it based on solidified fraction measurements from sampling volumes placed at key positions in the mold. This allows the simulation to replicate the closed-loop control used in real continuous casting machines without prescribing a fixed withdrawal profile.

*Active simulation control functionalities have been extended to include phantom objects, commonly used for continuous casting and additive manufacturing applications, as well as for cooling channels, used in casting and in many other thermal management applications.*
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Continuous Casting

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Additive Manufacturing

In directed energy deposition and other additive manufacturing processes, phantom components represent the substrate or the build volume being deposited layer by layer. Active Simulation Control manages the velocity of these phantom components dynamically, allowing the simulation to track the advancing build front in response to process conditions rather than following a fixed motion profile.
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Additive Manufacturing

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Water and Environmental Engineering

Control gates in fish passages and hydraulic structures must respond to flow velocity measurements to maintain acceptable conditions for passage. Active Simulation Control can move gates or adjust boundary conditions based on velocity readings at probes located in fish resting areas or downstream monitoring points. In reservoir and dam simulations, Active Simulation Control can control spillway gates based on water surface elevation probes.
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Water and Environmental Engineering

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Aerospace and Cryogenics

Cryogenic propellant tanks must maintain ullage pressure within tight bounds throughout operation. Active Simulation Control can trigger pressurization when ullage pressure drops below a threshold and shut it off when the target is reached, accurately simulating the on/off cycling of pressurization systems without manual intervention between runs.

*In this example, a pump (dark grey rectangle) in a cryogenic tank feed pipe pulls liquid oxygen from a propellant tank at a constant flow rate. As the liquid oxygen drains, a mass/momentum source (grey bar at top) is triggered by Active Simulation Control when the pressure in the ullage drops below a specified value. Pressurization is turned off when the ullage pressure rises above a specified value.*
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Aerospace and Cryogenics

text:
Active Simulation Control > Applications > Filling and Mixing

In filling and mixing applications, Active Simulation Control can sequence multi-stage operations: detecting when a fill level is reached, retracting the filler tube, lowering the mixer, and starting rotation, all within a single simulation run. Probe variables attached to moving objects track their position and trigger the next stage automatically.

*Active Simulation Control sequences a filling and mixing operation in **FLOW-3D**. The filler tube (pink) retracts when the fill level is reached, the mixing impeller (yellow) lowers into the fluid, and rotation begins when the impeller reaches its target depth. Marker dye concentration shows the mixing progress.*
heading: Active Simulation Control > Applications > Filling and Mixing

text:
Grid Overlay Procedure

The Grid Overlay procedure allows users to check the effects of grid refinement or to efficiently compute problems in which the region of interest is progressively decreasing or increasing, e.g., an explosion. For steady-state results a coarse grid might first be used to rough out a solution and then be replaced by a fine grid using the grid overlay procedure to give an accurate final answer.
heading: Grid Overlay Procedure

text:
Grid Overlay Procedure > Inkjet Example Using Grid Overlay

An example of the grid overlay procedure is shown in the accompanying figure of an inkjet device (left and middle). The computation started with a nozzle/piston assembly. After the jet is detached a new grid is used (right) to track its subsequent development. Additional grids can be used to follow the development of the moving jet for as long as desired. Using a grid overlay requires no special effort on the part of the user since the program does this automatically when restarting a simulation.

The grid overlay procedure is a powerful option in ***FLOW-3D*** that allows users to change the gridding of a computation while it is in progress. A new grid may be defined completely independently of the original grid. The new grid, for example, may be finer or coarser and it may overlay all or only a portion of the old grid.
heading: Grid Overlay Procedure > Inkjet Example Using Grid Overlay

text:
Grid Overlay Procedure > Grid Overlay Boundary Conditions

One useful application of the Grid Overlay Procedure is to perform a simulation that generates a flow profile for use in another simulation as a boundary condition. For example, steady laminar or turbulent flow in a pipe can be first simulated then used to start a second simulation with the end of the pipe flow grid overlaid on the inflow grid region of a second simulation requiring this profile as an inflow boundary condition. When the second simulation is restarted from the first simulation the solver will automatically check for any grid overlay regions and do the necessary transfer of data from the first to the second grid.
heading: Grid Overlay Procedure > Grid Overlay Boundary Conditions

text:
Core Gas > Core Gas Model

In sand casting, resin-bonded cores are used to create internal cavities and complex passages in the final part. When molten metal surrounds a core, the heat drives thermal decomposition of the organic binder, releasing gas. If that gas cannot escape fast enough through the core and its vents, the pressure builds until it overcomes the ferrostatic pressure of the metal at the core surface, and gas enters the casting as porosity or blow defects.

The Core Gas Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** predicts the generation and flow of binder gas within permeable sand cores and molds during and after mold filling. It gives foundry engineers a detailed, quantitative view of where gas is generated, how it moves through the core, and where it is most likely to enter the metal, enabling better core venting design before any metal is poured.
heading: Core Gas > Core Gas Model

text:
Core Gas > Core Gas Model > How the Model Works

The Core Gas Model treats the sand core as a porous medium through which compressible gas can be generated, flow, and exit. The conversion of solid binder to gas is described by an Arrhenius reaction rate equation, meaning gas generation accelerates rapidly as the core heats up. The generated gas is treated as compressible and ideal, governed by the ideal gas law with a gas constant determined from the binder chemistry.

Gas flow through the core is governed by Darcy’s law for flow in porous media. The metal pressure distribution at the outer surface of the core acts as a boundary condition for the gas flow: gas can escape into the metal when its pressure exceeds the local metal pressure, but once the metal has solidified at the core surface, no further gas exchange occurs at that location.

Because gas flow in cores can be much faster than the metal filling, ***FLOW-3D* CAST** employs a sub-time-stepping scheme for the core gas solver, allowing accurate gas computation without slowing down the overall filling simulation. A sub-cell resolution method is also used to accurately capture the steep thermal gradients in the thin binder decomposition zone at the core surface, which is typically only 0.25 to 0.5 mm wide.
heading: Core Gas > Core Gas Model > How the Model Works

text:
Core Gas > Core Gas Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Core Gas Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** computes:

- Binder gas generation rate as a function of local core temperature, using an Arrhenius decomposition model
- Gas flow through the core based on Darcy’s law, with permeability defined by average sand grain diameter or directly by Darcian and non-Darcian permeability values
- Gas pressure, density, and velocity distribution within the core, including thermal expansion of initial air as the core heats up
- Gas flux at the core surface, distinguishing between gas that escapes to void regions, gas that enters the metal, and gas that exits through print vents
- Venting at print surfaces, where gas escapes to atmosphere through the parting plane or through dedicated mold vents
- Metal pressure as a boundary condition for gas flow, updated in real time as filling progresses
- Total gasification rate and mass and volume flux history for each core component, available for postprocessing
heading: Core Gas > Core Gas Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Core Gas > Core Gas Model > Applications

Core gas defects are a persistent challenge in sand casting of both ferrous and non-ferrous alloys. The model is used to:

- Predict blowhole and gas porosity defects before committing to tooling
- Evaluate and optimize core vent placement and sizing
- Assess the effect of binder type and content on gas generation
- Compare vented and unvented core designs for complex assemblies such as water jacket cores in engine blocks
- Diagnose gas defects in existing castings by simulating the as-built core geometry and venting configuration
- Design core print geometry to ensure adequate gas escape paths
heading: Core Gas > Core Gas Model > Applications

text:
Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model

As castings grow more complex and wall sections thicker, shrinkage porosity in hard-to-feed areas can become unavoidable even with optimized gating, risering, and die temperature management. In high pressure and permanent mold casting, squeeze pins are a proven tool for addressing this problem: hydraulically actuated pins that press into the solidifying metal to compensate for shrinkage volume and reduce or eliminate porosity in targeted locations.

The Squeeze Pins Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** simulates the behavior of squeeze pins during solidification, allowing engineers to evaluate pin placement, sizing, timing, and activation strategy before committing to tooling. The effectiveness of squeeze pins is highly dependent on getting these parameters right, and simulation is the most practical way to explore the design space.
heading: Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model

text:
Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > How the Model Works

The Squeeze Pins Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** is based on the prescribed-motion General Moving Objects model and works in conjunction with the Simple Shrinkage Model. Once activated, a squeeze pin senses the amount of shrinkage in the adjacent liquid metal and moves in to exactly compensate for that volume. The pin advances along a defined line of action until it either reaches its maximum travel distance or encounters sufficient solidified metal on its working surface to prevent further movement.

A force can be specified for each pin, which is translated into metal pressure. This pressure can be coupled with the Thermal Stress Evolution Model and Porosity Formation Model to predict the effect of intensification pressure on residual stress and porosity distribution in the solidified casting.

The shot sleeve plunger can also be defined as a squeeze pin during solidification, allowing the model to capture the effect of intensification pressure applied through the plunger after cavity fill is complete.
heading: Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > How the Model Works

text:
Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Activation Control

Squeeze pin timing is critical. A pin activated too early may push metal out of the cavity through an unsealed gate. A pin activated too late may encounter too much solidified metal to move effectively. The Squeeze Pins Model offers three activation modes to support both the design stage and production validation:

- User-prescribed time: the pin activates at a specified time, suitable when timing has been determined from prior simulations or process experience
- Automatic activation: the pin activates when the adjacent liquid metal is sufficiently isolated from free surfaces, preventing metal from being pushed out of the cavity. The automatic mode also checks that the pin is not connected to another pin through a contiguous liquid path, avoiding competition between pins. This mode is most useful during the design stage when exact timing is not yet known
- Active Simulation Control: the pin activation is controlled by simulation state variables at specified locations in the casting, allowing the user to replicate the logic of the actual squeeze pin control system on the die casting machine
heading: Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Activation Control

text:
Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Case Study: Two-Cavity HPDC

A case study was carried out on a two-cavity high pressure die casting (HPDC) to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Squeeze Pins Model. Two sets of simulations were run: one without squeeze pins and one with squeeze pins configured at the locations identified as most prone to shrinkage porosity. The simulations without squeeze pins predicted significant porosity in the thick sections of the casting. With squeeze pins activated at the optimal time, the model predicted a substantial reduction in porosity at those locations, consistent with what is observed in physical production with squeeze pins engaged.
heading: Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Case Study: Two-Cavity HPDC

text:
Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Applications

The Squeeze Pins Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** is used to:

- Determine optimal squeeze pin placement to target shrinkage porosity in thick or isolated casting sections
- Evaluate pin timing to maximize effectiveness without risk of pushing metal through unsealed gates
- Size squeeze pin force and travel to achieve target metal pressure at the defect location
- Assess the effect of intensification pressure on porosity and residual stress using coupled models
- Replicate the squeeze pin control logic from the die casting machine to validate the production process
- Compare design alternatives for pin layout on complex multi-cavity dies
heading: Squeeze Pins > Squeeze Pins Model > Applications

text:
Cooling and Feeding System Design

Shrinkage porosity is one of the most common defects in metal castings. As metal solidifies and contracts, regions that freeze last can develop voids if there is no pathway for liquid metal to feed in and compensate for the volume loss. Designing an effective feeding system means knowing where those last-to-freeze regions will be, and ensuring that risers are sized and positioned to feed them before they are isolated by surrounding solid metal.

The Cooling and Feeding System Design tools in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** give casting engineers two powerful diagnostics to guide riser and chill placement: the Last Places to Freeze map and the Thermal Modulus calculation. Both are generated automatically from a solidification simulation, turning the simulation results directly into actionable design guidance.
heading: Cooling and Feeding System Design

text:
Cooling and Feeding System Design > Last Places to Freeze

The Last Places to Freeze tool identifies and visualizes the locations in the casting that solidify after all their neighboring regions. These hot spots mark exactly where shrinkage porosity is most likely to form. Rather than requiring engineers to interpret solidification time contours manually, ***FLOW-3D* CAST** places particles automatically at each hot spot location as it forms during the simulation.

Each hot spot particle carries attributes that quantify the risk at that location: the cell solidification time, a sequential hot spot ID showing the order in which regions froze, and the local thermal modulus. Together these give engineers a clear, ranked view of where feeding is most critical and which locations are at greatest risk of defect formation.
heading: Cooling and Feeding System Design > Last Places to Freeze

text:
Cooling and Feeding System Design > Thermal Modulus

Thermal modulus is a well-established method for riser design in foundry practice. The principle is straightforward: a riser must solidify later than the section it is feeding, so the riser needs to be designed with a larger modulus than the casting section it serves. Modulus is essentially the ratio of a section’s volume to its cooling surface area. A thick, enclosed section cools slowly and has a high modulus; a thin fin cools fast and has a low modulus. Because modulus is a geometric quantity, comparing moduli is simpler and more direct than comparing solidification times.

What makes ***FLOW-3D* CAST**’s Thermal Modulus tool particularly powerful is that it goes beyond simple geometry. Rather than computing modulus from shape alone, it derives an equivalent thermal modulus from the actual solidification simulation, which already accounts for the effects of chills, insulating risers, exothermic sleeves, and variable heat transfer across the mold. This means the thermal modulus map reflects real process conditions, not just the casting geometry in isolation.

The result is a spatial map of modulus values across the casting that engineers can directly compare against riser modulus to validate feeding system designs. Regions where the casting modulus is high relative to neighboring areas indicate potential feeding challenges that need riser coverage.
heading: Cooling and Feeding System Design > Thermal Modulus

text:
Cooling and Feeding System Design > Case Study: Steam Turbine Cylinder

A case study demonstrating the Cooling and Feeding System Design tools was carried out for the gravity casting of half a steam turbine cylinder, courtesy of Flow Science China. The outer dimensions of the part are approximately 2.83 x 2.34 x 1.10 m, making it a large and complex casting where manual riser design would be extremely difficult.
heading: Cooling and Feeding System Design > Case Study: Steam Turbine Cylinder

text:
Cooling and Feeding System Design > Applications

The Cooling and Feeding System Design tools are used in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** for:

- Identifying hot spot locations to guide riser placement in gravity, permanent mold, and sand casting
- Sizing risers using thermal modulus to ensure proper feeding without oversized, wasteful risers
- Evaluating the effect of chills and insulating risers on the solidification sequence
- Comparing alternative feeding system designs to select the most efficient option
- Diagnosing shrinkage porosity defects in existing castings by mapping the solidification sequence
- Supporting casting design for large, complex parts where manual feeding analysis is impractical
heading: Cooling and Feeding System Design > Applications

text:
Dissolving Objects Model

When a solid dissolves in a liquid, the flow domain changes shape, and the dissolved material redistributes through diffusion and convection. ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** include a fully coupled Dissolving Objects Model that captures the dissolution process, the changing geometry of the solid, and the transport of the solute in the fluid.
heading: Dissolving Objects Model

text:
Dissolving Objects Model > How It Works

The dissolution is driven by the difference between the local concentration and the saturation concentration of the solute: dissolution proceeds faster where the fluid is less saturated and slows as the surrounding fluid approaches saturation.

The solute is transported through the fluid by convection and diffusion. At the boundary between the solid and the fluid, the dissolution rate is controlled by the rate of diffusion of the solute away from the interface. If diffusion is relatively slow, for example, fluid in the boundary layer becomes saturated stopping further dissolution.

As the solid dissolves, it decreases in size, and its shape changes as well. The area and volume fractions are recomputed at every time step to reflect the gradual loss of the solid material, allowing the flow domain to expand. The mixture densityvaries as a function of the solute concentration, affecting buoyancy.

The model supports both *interstitial* solutes, where smaller solute molecules fit into the spaces between the molecules of the solvent with little change in the mixture volume, and *substitutional* solutes, where larger solute molecules displace the solvent ones increasing the mixture volume. A configurable density mixing coefficient covers the range between these two cases, allowing the model to be calibrated to the physical behavior of specific solute-solvent pairs.
heading: Dissolving Objects Model > How It Works

text:
Dissolving Objects Model > How It Works > Example: Salt Block Dissolution

The images below show a case in which solid medicine dissolves in flowing water. The computational domain contains a bed of cylindrical pins arranged in a regular array sandwiched between two flat plates with the dissolvable tablet placed in the middle. Fluid enters from one end of the domain at a constant rate and leaves at the opposite side. The flow is confined. As dissolution proceeds, the tablet reduces in size and the dissolved substance is carried downstream by the flow.
heading: Dissolving Objects Model > How It Works > Example: Salt Block Dissolution

text:
Dissolving Objects Model > Applications

The Dissolving Objects Model applies across a wide range of industries and problem types:

- **Solution mining** for simulating the dissolution of salt or mineral deposits by injected fluid to create underground cavities for resource extraction or energy storage
- **Underground gas storage** for modeling the creation of salt caverns used for natural gas and compressed air energy storage
- **Drug delivery and controlled release** for predicting dissolution rates of pharmaceutical coatings and solid drug forms in biological fluids
- **Environmental and water quality** for simulating dissolution of soluble materials in natural water systems, including contaminant release scenarios
heading: Dissolving Objects Model > Applications

text:
Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model

Many engineering flows involve a mixture of two fluids with different densities, such as air and water or oil and water, where one component is dispersed as droplets or bubbles within the other. In these flows, the size of the dispersed fluid elements is not fixed; droplets break up under shear forces and coalesce when they collide. The evolving size distribution affects how quickly the droplets rise or settle, how they interact with turbulence, and how the mixture as a whole behaves. ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** include a Dynamic Droplet Model that tracks the evolution of dispersed droplet or bubble size throughout the simulation, providing a more physically realistic representation of two-fluid mixtures.

*Oil droplets coalesce into larger droplets downstream of the energy dissipation plate, increasing buoyancy and allowing the oil to rise over the weir into the collection pipe.*
heading: Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model

text:
Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model > How It Works

The Dynamic Droplet Model is an extension of the Drift Flux Model, which handles the relative motion between the dispersed and continuous phases due to buoyancy and viscous forces. This model accounts for the effect of breakup and coalesce on the evolution of the droplet or bubble size. The balance between these two competing mechanisms determines the local equilibrium droplet diameter at each point in the flow, which varies spatially and temporally as flow conditions change.

Because droplet size directly determines the drag force and therefore the drift velocity of the dispersed phase, a more accurate size prediction leads to more accurate predictions of phase separation, bubble rise rates, and the distribution of the dispersed phase throughout the fluid.
heading: Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model > How It Works

text:
Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model > Applications

The Dynamic Droplet Model extends the two-component flow capabilities of ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** to problems where droplet or bubble size evolution matters:

- **Spillway and chute aeration** for predicting the spatial distribution and size of entrained air bubbles in high-velocity flows over hydraulic structures
- **Oil-water separation** for modeling the breakup and coalescence of oil droplets in water as they move through separators, pipes, and process vessels
- **Bubble column reactors** for predicting bubble size distribution and its effect on mass transfer and mixing performance in chemical and biological reactors
- **Liquid-liquid extraction** for simulating the dispersal and coalescence of droplets in extraction columns and mixing-settling devices
- **Emulsification and mixing** for evaluating the effect of impeller geometry and operating speed on droplet size distribution in industrial mixing processes
- **Aerated flows in hydraulic structures** for assessing bubble size distributions in stilling basins, drop structures, and plunge pools where aeration affects energy dissipation and dissolved oxygen transfer

*A bottle filling example uses the dynamic droplet model for highly viscous flows. These results compare three simulations that use different values of the critical capillary number, which defines the necessary shear stress for droplet breakup.*
heading: Dynamic Droplet Model for Two-Component Flows > Dynamic Droplet Model > Applications

text:
CFD Glossary

Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) draws on a broad set of physical principles and numerical techniques. This glossary defines the foundational terms engineers encounter when building, running, and interpreting CFD simulations in the ***FLOW-3D*** family of products, covering fluid physics, numerical methods, turbulence modeling, and free-surface tracking, including the proprietary technologies that power the solver.
heading: CFD Glossary

text:
CFD Glossary > Advection

The transport of a fluid property (such as heat, concentration, or momentum) by the bulk motion of the fluid. Advection is one of the primary mechanisms by which quantities move through the computational domain and appears as a key term in the governing transport equations.
heading: CFD Glossary > Advection

text:
CFD Glossary > Boundary conditions

Mathematical constraints applied at the edges of the computational domain that define the state of the flow at those locations. Common types include inflow/outflow, pressure, wall, and symmetry conditions. The accuracy of a simulation depends heavily on selecting boundary conditions that reflect real physical conditions.
heading: CFD Glossary > Boundary conditions

text:
CFD Glossary > Boundary layer

The thin region of fluid immediately adjacent to a solid surface where viscous effects are significant and velocity transitions from zero at the wall to the free-stream value. Boundary layer behavior determines wall shear stress, heat transfer rates, and the onset of flow separation.
heading: CFD Glossary > Boundary layer

text:
CFD Glossary > Cavitation

Mathematical constraints applied at the edges of the computational domain that define the state of the flow at those locations. Common types include inflow/outflow, pressure, wall, and symmetry conditions. The accuracy of a simulation depends heavily on selecting boundary conditions that reflect real physical conditions.
heading: CFD Glossary > Cavitation

text:
CFD Glossary > CFD

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is the branch of fluid mechanics that uses numerical methods and algorithms to simulate and analyze fluid flow, heat transfer, and related physical phenomena on a computer.
heading: CFD Glossary > CFD

text:
CFD Glossary > Compressible flow

A flow regime in which the fluid density changes significantly due to pressure or temperature variations, most commonly encountered in high-speed gas flows. When density changes are negligible, the flow is treated as incompressible.
heading: CFD Glossary > Compressible flow

text:
CFD Glossary > Contact angle

The angle at which a fluid interface meets a solid surface, measured through the liquid. Contact angle determines how a fluid wets a surface and significantly influences free-surface behavior at walls, particularly in capillary-driven and low-gravity flows.
heading: CFD Glossary > Contact angle

text:
CFD Glossary > Continuity equation

A mathematical expression of the conservation of mass, stating that for an incompressible fluid the net volumetric flow rate into any control volume must equal zero. ***FLOW-3D*** enforces continuity iteratively at each time step through pressure/velocity coupling.
heading: CFD Glossary > Continuity equation

text:
CFD Glossary > Convergence

The process by which an iterative numerical solution approaches a stable, self-consistent result. A solution is considered converged when residuals (the imbalance remaining in the governing equations) fall below a specified tolerance at each time step.
heading: CFD Glossary > Convergence

text:
CFD Glossary > Courant number

A dimensionless number that relates the time-step size to the mesh cell size and local fluid velocity. The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition requires the Courant number to remain at or below a threshold value to ensure numerical stability in explicit time-stepping schemes.
heading: CFD Glossary > Courant number

text:
CFD Glossary > Diffusion

The spreading of a quantity (such as heat, mass, or momentum) from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration driven by molecular or turbulent mixing. Diffusion terms appear alongside advection terms in the transport equations governing fluid behavior.
heading: CFD Glossary > Diffusion

text:
CFD Glossary > Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS)

A CFD approach in which all scales of turbulent motion are resolved directly without a turbulence model, requiring an extremely fine mesh and small time steps. DNS is computationally prohibitive for most engineering problems and is primarily used for fundamental turbulence research.
heading: CFD Glossary > Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS)

text:
CFD Glossary > Discretization

The process of converting continuous governing equations into a set of algebraic equations solvable on a finite mesh. ***FLOW-3D*** uses a finite difference approach applied to a structured rectangular mesh, with the FAVOR™ method used to represent complex geometry within that mesh.
heading: CFD Glossary > Discretization

text:
CFD Glossary > Domain

The bounded region in space in which the governing equations are solved, defined by the extents of the computational mesh. Proper domain sizing ensures that boundary conditions do not artificially influence the flow in the region of interest.
heading: CFD Glossary > Domain

text:
CFD Glossary > FAVOR™

Fractional Area/Volume Obstacle Representation. A proprietary method used by ***FLOW-3D*** to represent complex geometry on a structured rectangular mesh by computing the fractional open areas and volumes of each computational cell. FAVOR™ allows accurate representation of curved and irregular surfaces without requiring a body-fitted or unstructured mesh.
heading: CFD Glossary > FAVOR™

text:
CFD Glossary > Finite difference method

A numerical technique that approximates derivatives in the governing equations by computing algebraic differences between values at discrete mesh points. ***FLOW-3D***'s solver is based on a finite difference formulation applied to a structured rectangular grid.
heading: CFD Glossary > Finite difference method

text:
CFD Glossary > Finite volume method

A numerical approach that discretizes the governing equations by integrating them over control volumes surrounding each mesh cell. The finite volume method inherently conserves mass, momentum, and energy across cell boundaries, making it widely used in commercial CFD solvers.
heading: CFD Glossary > Finite volume method

text:
CFD Glossary > Free surface

The bounded region in space in which the governing equations are solved, defined by the extents of the computational mesh. Proper domain sizing ensures that boundary conditions do not artificially influence the flow in the region of interest.
heading: CFD Glossary > Free surface

text:
CFD Glossary > Incompressible flow

A flow in which fluid density is assumed constant throughout the domain, regardless of pressure variations. Most liquid flows and low-speed gas flows are treated as incompressible. The incompressible assumption simplifies the governing equations and is the default in most ***FLOW-3D*** simulations.
heading: CFD Glossary > Incompressible flow

text:
CFD Glossary > k-epsilon turbulence model

A widely used two-equation RANS turbulence model that solves transport equations for turbulent kinetic energy (k) and its dissipation rate (epsilon) to compute an effective turbulent viscosity. ***FLOW-3D*** offers both the standard k-epsilon and the RNG k-epsilon variant, which provides improved accuracy for flows with high strain rates and recirculation.
heading: CFD Glossary > k-epsilon turbulence model

text:
CFD Glossary > Laminar flow

A smooth, ordered flow regime in which fluid moves in parallel layers with minimal mixing between them. Laminar flow occurs at low Reynolds numbers where viscous forces dominate over inertial forces. The transition to turbulence depends on geometry, velocity, and fluid properties.
heading: CFD Glossary > Laminar flow

text:
CFD Glossary > Large Eddy Simulation (LES)

A turbulence modeling approach that directly resolves large-scale turbulent eddies while modeling the effects of smaller sub-grid-scale eddies. In comparison to RANS-based models, LES can provide instantaneous information about the flow and can be more accurate for flows with complex, anisotropic turbulence; but requires significantly more computational resources.
heading: CFD Glossary > Large Eddy Simulation (LES)

text:
CFD Glossary > Mesh

The discrete spatial framework that divides the computational domain into a finite number of cells. ***FLOW-3D*** uses a structured rectangular mesh, in which cells are organized in regular rows and columns. Mesh resolution directly affects simulation accuracy, with finer cells resolving smaller flow features at greater computational cost.
heading: CFD Glossary > Mesh

text:
CFD Glossary > Mesh convergence study

A systematic process of progressively refining the computational mesh and repeating the simulation to verify that results no longer change significantly with further refinement. A mesh-converged solution indicates that discretization errors are acceptably small and results are reliable.
heading: CFD Glossary > Mesh convergence study

text:
CFD Glossary > Navier-Stokes equations

The fundamental partial differential equations governing the motion of viscous fluids, expressing the conservation of momentum. Combined with the continuity equation and, where relevant, the energy equation, the Navier-Stokes equations form the mathematical foundation of all CFD simulation.
heading: CFD Glossary > Navier-Stokes equations

text:
CFD Glossary > Numerical diffusion

Artificial smearing of sharp gradients introduced by truncation errors in the discretization scheme. Numerical diffusion can reduce accuracy near interfaces and sharp flow features. ***FLOW-3D***'s **TruVOF** method is specifically designed to minimize numerical diffusion at free surfaces.
heading: CFD Glossary > Numerical diffusion

text:
CFD Glossary > Pressure-velocity coupling

The numerical procedure used to enforce consistency between the pressure and velocity fields in an incompressible flow solver. Because pressure does not have its own transport equation in incompressible flow, iterative methods are required to ensure that the computed velocity field satisfies continuity at every time step.
heading: CFD Glossary > Pressure-velocity coupling

text:
CFD Glossary > Reynolds number

A dimensionless number expressing the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow. Low Reynolds numbers indicate laminar flow; high values indicate turbulent flow. Reynolds number is a fundamental parameter for characterizing flow regime and for scaling experimental results to simulation conditions.
heading: CFD Glossary > Reynolds number

text:
CFD Glossary > Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS)

An approach to turbulence modeling in which the Navier-Stokes equations are averaged, decomposing flow variables into mean and fluctuating components. RANS models, including k-epsilon and RNG k-epsilon, solve for the mean flow and model the effect of turbulence through an additional turbulent viscosity term.
heading: CFD Glossary > Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS)

text:
CFD Glossary > Sharp interface

A free-surface representation in which the transition between fluid and void is confined to a single cell face rather than smeared over multiple cells. Sharp interface methods preserve physical accuracy at the fluid boundary, particularly for wave dynamics, jetting, and droplet formation.
heading: CFD Glossary > Sharp interface

text:
CFD Glossary > Steady state

A flow condition in which all quantities at every point in the domain remain constant over time. Many engineering flows are analyzed at steady state to reduce computational cost. Where flow is inherently unsteady (such as in filling, sloshing, or turbulent recirculation) a transient simulation is required.
heading: CFD Glossary > Steady state

text:
CFD Glossary > Surface tension

The cohesive intermolecular force at the interface between a liquid and a gas that acts to minimize surface area. Surface tension drives capillary rise, droplet formation, and interface stability, and is particularly significant in small-scale flows where it dominates over gravitational and inertial forces.
heading: CFD Glossary > Surface tension

text:
CFD Glossary > Transient simulation

A simulation that resolves how flow conditions evolve over time, rather than converging to a single steady-state solution. ***FLOW-3D*** is inherently a transient solver, tracking free-surface motion, filling, and other time-dependent phenomena from start to finish.
heading: CFD Glossary > Transient simulation

text:
CFD Glossary > TruVOF

Flow Science's proprietary implementation of the volume-of-fluid method for tracking free surfaces. **TruVOF** maintains a sharp fluid interface confined to a single cell face, preventing the numerical diffusion that degrades accuracy in standard VOF implementations. This precision is central to ***FLOW-3D***'s ability to accurately simulate wave dynamics, jetting, splashing, and free-surface filling.
heading: CFD Glossary > TruVOF

text:
CFD Glossary > Turbulence

A chaotic, unsteady flow regime characterized by eddies, vortices, and rapid fluctuations in velocity and pressure. Turbulence occurs at high Reynolds numbers when inertial forces overwhelm viscous damping. Because resolving all turbulent scales directly is computationally prohibitive for most engineering flows, turbulence models are used to represent its effects on the mean flow.
heading: CFD Glossary > Turbulence

text:
CFD Glossary > Turbulent kinetic energy

A measure of the energy contained in turbulent velocity fluctuations, typically denoted k. It is one of the two transported quantities in the standard k-epsilon and RNG k-epsilon turbulence models, and is used to compute the turbulent viscosity that augments molecular viscosity in the momentum equations.
heading: CFD Glossary > Turbulent kinetic energy

text:
CFD Glossary > Validation

The process of demonstrating that a simulation model accurately represents real physical behavior by comparing results against experimental measurements or physical observations. Validation establishes credibility for a simulation's intended use and is distinct from verification.
heading: CFD Glossary > Validation

text:
CFD Glossary > Verification

The process of confirming that a simulation correctly solves the governing equations as intended, typically through comparison with analytical solutions or established benchmarks. A verified simulation may still require validation against experimental data to confirm physical accuracy.
heading: CFD Glossary > Verification

text:
CFD Glossary > Viscosity

A measure of a fluid's resistance to deformation under shear stress. Dynamic viscosity quantifies the absolute resistance to flow; kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by fluid density. Viscosity governs boundary layer thickness, flow regime, and the balance between viscous and inertial forces expressed by the Reynolds number.
heading: CFD Glossary > Viscosity

text:
CFD Glossary > Volume of fluid (VOF)

A numerical method for tracking free surfaces by computing the fraction of each mesh cell occupied by a given fluid. A cell value of 1 indicates fully fluid, 0 indicates void, and intermediate values mark the interface region. ***FLOW-3D***'s **TruVOF** method extends the standard VOF approach to maintain a sharp, single-cell-face interface.
heading: CFD Glossary > Volume of fluid (VOF)

text:
CFD Glossary > Vorticity

A vector quantity describing the local rotation rate of the fluid, defined as the curl of the velocity field. Vorticity is used in post-processing to identify vortex structures, recirculation zones, and turbulent flow features that may not be apparent from velocity or pressure fields alone.
heading: CFD Glossary > Vorticity

text:
CFD Glossary > Wall functions

Empirical relationships used to approximate the flow behavior in the near-wall boundary layer without resolving it with a fine mesh. Wall functions reduce mesh requirements near solid surfaces by bridging between the wall and the fully turbulent outer flow, and are used in conjunction with RANS turbulence models in ***FLOW-3D***. Also known as wall models.
heading: CFD Glossary > Wall functions

text:
CFD Glossary > Wall shear stress

The tangential force per unit area exerted by the fluid on a solid surface, arising from the velocity gradient in the boundary layer. Wall shear stress is relevant for erosion prediction, drag calculations, and no-slip boundary condition modeling.
heading: CFD Glossary > Wall shear stress

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model

Between shots in high pressure die casting, spray robots traverse the open die with banks of nozzles that apply lubricant and coolant to the die surface. This spray cooling step is one of the most important thermal management tools available to the die caster. Where the spray lands, how long it is applied, and which areas are blocked by die geometry all have a direct effect on die temperature distribution, hot spot behavior, and ultimately casting quality and die life.

The Die Spray Cooling Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** simulates the spatial variation in spray cooling across the die surface during thermal die cycling simulations. Rather than applying a constant heat transfer coefficient to the entire cavity, the model explicitly computes the cooling effect of each spray nozzle, accounting for nozzle position and movement, spray cone geometry, die surface shape, and blockage effects. This produces a realistic, spatially varying temperature distribution that reflects the actual spray process.
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > How the Model Works

The model uses a ray tracing algorithm to compute the spray area on the die surface in real time as the spray robot moves. For each nozzle and die surface element, the model determines whether the element is within the spray cone, whether it is blocked by die geometry, and whether it receives spray from multiple overlapping nozzles. Areas blocked from the spray receive only the ambient heat transfer coefficient; areas sprayed by multiple nozzles receive the highest applicable heat transfer coefficient.

Nozzles are grouped into banks, each with its own spray cone characteristics, coolant properties, and on/off control schedule. The translational and rotational movement of the spray robot arm is defined as a time-dependent motion table, allowing the full traversal path to be captured accurately.
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model > How the Model Works

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation

Two methods are available for defining the spray cooling heat transfer coefficient (HTC), giving engineers flexibility based on the data available to them.
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation > Dependency-Based Method

When the spatial variation of the HTC is known from measurement or prior CFD analysis, it can be expressed as a base HTC multiplied by factors that account for spray distance, spray angles, and other spatial dependencies. These factor functions can be defined as constants or tabular data, and can be linked to external files for ease of management across multiple nozzle configurations.
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation > Dependency-Based Method

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation > Spray Medium Properties Method

When spatial HTC data is not available, the model can compute the heat transfer coefficient directly from spray medium properties. The calculation is based on the energy exchange between the spray and the die surface, accounting for the spray nozzle flow rate, coolant density and evaporation temperature, spray cone geometry, spray distance, and spray angles. A calibration efficiency coefficient (default 0.75) can be adjusted to match experimental temperature measurements. This method makes the Die Spray Cooling Model practical for foundries that do not have access to detailed spray characterization data.
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model > Heat Transfer Coefficient Calculation > Spray Medium Properties Method

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Die Spray Cooling Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** supports:

- Ray tracing computation of spray area on the die surface, updated continuously as the robot moves
- Blockage detection based on die surface shape and spray angle
- Overlap handling for areas covered by multiple spray nozzles
- Multiple nozzle banks with independent spray characteristics, coolant properties, and on/off schedules
- Time-dependent robot arm motion (translational and rotational) defined as a motion table
- Two HTC calculation methods: spatial dependency functions or spray medium properties
- Nozzle database for storing and reusing characterized nozzle properties across simulations
- Spray area visualization output for validating nozzle positioning and robot path
- Total spray time and total heat removed per unit area for postprocessing
- Integration with Thermal Die Cycling for multi-cycle die temperature analysis
- Part-by-part spray treatment schedules with options for spraying, cleaning, and coating defined independently per die component
- Slider motion support, with cooling channels and heating elements moving with sliders during the spray stage
heading: Die Spray Cooling Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Die Spray Cooling Model > Case Study: Structural Vehicle Component

A case study was carried out using a large, thin-walled structural vehicle component to demonstrate the importance of simulating die spraying explicitly rather than assuming a uniform heat transfer coefficient. The simulation used five thermal die cycles, each consisting of four stages: solidification, ejection, spray cooling, and dwelling.

Three thermocouples were placed in the ejector die to monitor temperature at different locations: one in the casting area, one outside the cavity where spray cooling occurs but no metal contact is made, and one at the biscuit, which acts as a hot spot. Comparing the thermocouple histories from the simulation against measured data demonstrated that the Die Spray Cooling Model produces significantly more accurate temperature predictions than a constant HTC approach, particularly at locations where spray geometry and blockage effects are significant.

text:
Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model

Many hydraulic engineering modeling problems required fully three dimensional simulations and span multiple length scales. A dam impounding a large reservoir, a bridge pier in a river, or a structure in an open coastal area all involve three-dimensional flow features embedded within a much larger domain. Flow in the larger domain may provide critical boundary condition information but may not always need to be simulated in three dimensions. In those cases, the computational expense of a large 3D model can be reduced with a Hybrid 2D/3D model

The Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** was developed specifically to improve modeling efficiency for this class of problems. In a single time step it combines the computational efficiency of shallow water (depth-averaged) equations with the local accuracy of full 3D Navier-Stokes equations where vertical flow structure matters. For example, engineers can model catchment-scale flood routing and a complex hydraulic structure in the same run.

The shallow water model can also be used alone (without a coupling with a 3D local model). This can be useful for preliminary screening of very large domains requiring a large number of scenarios, or for the generation of a hot start for a 3D model.

*Hybrid 3D/shallow water simulation of bridge hydraulics. The surrounding river reach is modeled with a 2D shallow water block; a nested 3D block resolves the velocity structure and flow details around the bridge piers. Color denotes velocity magnitude.*
heading: Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model

text:
Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model > How the Model Works

The model uses ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO**‘s multi-block meshing framework. Each mesh block is independently designated as a shallow water or 3D block. In shallow water blocks, the depth-averaged shallow water equations are solved for water surface elevation and depth-averaged velocities. In 3D blocks, the full unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations are solved, resolving the three velocity components, pressure and turbulence structures.

At the boundaries between adjacent or nested blocks, the solutions are coupled: the shallow water block provides boundary conditions for the 3D block, and the 3D block returns updated flow information to the shallow water block.

Blocks can be arranged in two configurations. Adjacent blocks share a face along their common boundary, suitable for transitioning from a shallow water domain to a 3D domain around a structure. Nested blocks place a 3D block entirely inside a shallow water block, drawing boundary conditions from the surrounding flow and feeding back into it.

In shallow water blocks, bed friction can be calculated using the Manning, Chezy, Strickler, Nikuradse , Colebrook-White, Haaland, Ramette and Soulsby log law formulations. Bed friction can be applied as a uniform value or mapped spatially from an external file, allowing realistic representation of floodplains with mixed land cover. Horizontal turbulent mixing in shallow water blocks is governed by a constant diffusivity, mixing length, or Smagorinsky sub-grid scale model. The Shallow Water Model does not need to be run in combination with a 3D mesh block.
heading: Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model > How the Model Works

text:
Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model > Simulation Examples > Thermal plume during a flood event

A thermal power plant discharges warm cooling water into a river. Locally, the outfall creates a concentrated buoyant plume that gradually mixes vertically and laterally. Because the river is shallow compared to its width, vertical mixing is quickly achieved while lateral mixing occurs over a larger domain. The nearfield discharge is modeled in 3D to capture the vertical breakup of the plume. Far field lateral mixing can be modeled with the shallow water model. The hybrid modeling approach allows better definition of the environmental impacts of the thermal plume and the benefits of better diffuser design.
heading: Hybrid Shallow Water/3D Flow Model > Simulation Examples > Thermal plume during a flood event
