text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model

Traditional casting simulation relies on tabular material properties (solidus and liquidus temperatures, latent heat, and density) provided by the user. These inputs work well for standard alloy grades but tell engineers nothing about how microstructure varies across the casting, how mechanical properties relate to local solidification conditions, or how alloy composition changes could improve performance.

The Chemistry-Based Solidification Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than requiring users to supply material properties, it computes the full solidification path from the alloy’s chemical composition, accounting for nucleation, segregation, and local cooling conditions at every point in the casting. The result is a simulation that predicts not just where metal solidifies, but what microstructure forms, what mechanical properties result, and where porosity is most likely, all as a direct output of the casting process.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > What the Model Predicts

Starting from alloy chemical composition, the Chemistry-Based Solidification Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** computes:

- Solidification path (solid fraction vs. temperature) based on nucleation, segregation, and cooling conditions, without requiring user-supplied tabular data
- All temperature-dependent material properties including latent heat, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, density, and viscosity, derived directly from the chemistry
- Microstructure features including secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) and grain size, based on local composition and cooling rate
- Macro-segregation due to diffusion and advection of solute elements in the liquid phase
- As-cast and heat-treated mechanical properties including yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation, based on empirical relationships between microstructure and mechanical performance (AlSi- and AlCu-based alloys)
- Microporosity using the dimensionless Niyama criterion, which is enabled by the chemistry-based solidification path
- Resolved shrinkage porosity with improved visualization of leak paths, in the EXODUS output format

The following examples show predicted elongation for an AlSi9Cu3(Fe) alloy casting, illustrating how the model maps mechanical properties and microstructure spatially across the part.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > What the Model Predicts

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models

The Chemistry-Based Solidification Model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** is available in two modes to balance accuracy with simulation efficiency.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models > Full Model

The Full Model tracks chemical composition and phase evolution in every computational cell throughout the simulation. This provides the most accurate prediction of macro-segregation, where solute redistribution due to convection and diffusion varies significantly across the casting. The Full Model requires more computation time and memory than the tabular approach, typically two to three times longer, and is recommended when macro-segregation is a primary concern.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models > Full Model

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models > Simplified Model

The Simplified Model pre-computes the solidification path and material properties in the preprocessor based on the alloy composition and chosen solute redistribution model, then applies them uniformly across the simulation. This gives users the full benefit of chemistry-based microstructure and mechanical property prediction with no additional runtime or memory cost compared to tabular input. For most thin-walled castings and fast-cooled parts where macro-segregation is not significant, the Simplified Model is the recommended choice.

The two modes can be combined within a workflow: a restart simulation can transition from the Full Model to the Simplified Model or vice versa, giving engineers the flexibility to use the most appropriate approach at each stage of the simulation.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Full and Simplified Models > Simplified Model

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Supported Alloys

The Chemistry-Based Solidification Model currently supports:

- Aluminum-silicon alloys (AlSi-based), covering the majority of commercial AlSi grades including A356 and similar alloys
- Aluminum-copper alloys (AlCu-based), including A206 and similar grades
- Carbon and low alloy steels (CLAS), with alloying elements C, Si, Mn, P, S, Cr, Mo, Ni, and Cu, using either equilibrium or Gulliver-Scheil solute redistribution

For aluminum alloys, the effect of grain refiners (Ti and Ti-B additions) is included in the model, assuming optimum addition for maximum grain refining effect.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Supported Alloys

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Validation

The aluminum-silicon and aluminum-copper alloy solidification model has been experimentally validated against A356 and A206 commercial ingots in collaboration with The University of Alabama at Birmingham. The results are detailed in a publication that received the Best Paper Award from the 2020 American Foundry Society Aluminum and Light Metals Division, confirming the accuracy of the microstructure and mechanical property predictions against measured experimental data.
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Validation

text:
Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Applications

The Chemistry-Based Solidification Model is used in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** to:

- Predict spatial variation in microstructure (SDAS, grain size) across a casting without physical sectioning
- Map as-cast and heat-treated mechanical properties to identify weak regions before physical testing (AlSi- and AlCu-based alloys)
- Evaluate the effect of alloy composition changes on microstructure and properties
- Predict microporosity using the dimensionless Niyama criterion, enabled by accurate solidification path computation
- Visualize resolved shrinkage porosity and potential leak paths in structural castings
- Optimize process parameters (pouring temperature, cooling rate, die temperature) for target mechanical property distributions (AlSi- and AlCu-based alloys)
- Support casting qualification by demonstrating predicted mechanical properties meet design requirements (AlSi- and AlCu-based alloys)
heading: Chemistry-Based Solidification Model > Applications

text:
Surface Tension Model

Surface tension is the cohesive force at a liquid-gas or liquid-liquid interface that causes the surface to behave like a stretched elastic membrane. At small scales it dominates over gravity and inertia, controlling droplet formation, capillary rise, wetting behavior, and bubble dynamics. At larger scales it plays a critical role in coating stability, melt pool behavior in additive manufacturing and welding, and propellant management in spacecraft fuel tanks.

One of the earliest physics models in ***FLOW-3D***, the Surface Tension Model has been continuously applied over decades across industries from microfluidics and inkjet printing to aerospace and additive manufacturing. It is available across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family for both single-fluid free-surface flows and two-fluid problems with a sharp interface.
heading: Surface Tension Model

text:
Surface Tension Model > Modeling Capabilities

The ***FLOW-3D*** Surface Tension model accurately computes:

- Surface tension forces at free surfaces and fluid-fluid interfaces
- Wall adhesion controlled by a global or geometry-specific contact angle
- Tangential surface tension forces caused by non-uniform surface tension coefficients due to temperature or concentration gradients
- Electrowetting effects, where an applied electric potential modifies the apparent contact angle
- Contact line pinning, which fixes the fluid contact line to a solid surface rather than computing its motion from a force balance. See the Contact Line Pinning Model for more information.

Surface tension coefficients can be defined as a constant, as a linear function of temperature, or using tabular data with up to two independent variables, for example temperature and contaminant concentration. This allows complex, non-linear property dependencies to be captured directly from experimental data, which is particularly valuable for surfactant-laden fluids, polymer solutions, and liquid metals.
heading: Surface Tension Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications

The Surface Tension Model is used across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family for applications including:

- Lab-on-a-chip, bioassay, and microreactor design
- Inkjet and drop-on-demand printing
- Roll, curtain, gravure, and slide coating processes
- Capillary filling and wicking in porous media
- Propellant management devices and fuel acquisition in microgravity
- Laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition melt pool dynamics
- Laser welding keyhole and bead geometry
- Electrowetting and digital microfluidics
- Droplet impact and spreading on substrates
- MEMS and micro-electromechanical device simulation
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Microfluidics and Lab-on-a-Chip

At the microscale, surface tension governs nearly everything. ***FLOW-3D*** is widely used to simulate lab-on-a-chip devices, bioassays, microreactors, and biological sensing systems where surface tension drives fluid transport, droplet generation, and capillary filling. Patterned surfaces with spatially varying wettability can be used to direct fluid flow in micro-channels without mechanical pumping, opening up new design possibilities for passive microfluidic systems.

**FLOW-3D** simulation of patterned surfaces using varied surface tensions, showing fluid 2 (top left) and fluid 1 (bottom left) distributions in a micro-channel, with pressure at inlet over time (right).
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Microfluidics and Lab-on-a-Chip

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Inkjet Printing and Drop-on-Demand

Surface tension governs the entire lifecycle of an inkjet droplet, from pinch-off at the nozzle to spreading and drying on the substrate. ***FLOW-3D*** simulates droplet formation, satellite behavior, and substrate interaction, giving engineers the insight needed to optimize nozzle geometry, fluid formulation, and firing parameters for consistent, accurate drop placement.

**FLOW-3D** simulation of piezoelectric inkjet droplet ejection, showing droplet velocity (left) alongside nozzle pressure pulse and volume flow rate time histories (right).
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Inkjet Printing and Drop-on-Demand

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Industrial Coating Processes

Surface tension is a primary driver of coating stability, defect formation, and contact line behavior. ***FLOW-3D*** is used to predict the onset of ribbing instabilities in roll coating, the stability of the dynamic contact line in curtain coating, and the entrainment of bubbles where the liquid front meets the substrate. The ability to capture spatially and thermally varying surface tension gives engineers accurate insight into real process conditions.

**FLOW-3D** simulation of a forward roll coating process showing a ribbing defect caused by a high capillary number, with surface tension and viscosity modeled through a 400 micron nip.
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Industrial Coating Processes

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Aerospace Propellant Management

In microgravity, surface tension controls the location and behavior of liquid propellants far more than gravity does. ***FLOW-3D*** simulates propellant management devices, capillary vanes, and sponge structures designed to guarantee vapor-free fuel delivery to engines during spacecraft maneuvers. Engineers use the model to assess fuel acquisition under orbit conditions and to validate tank designs before flight

*In microgravity, surface tension becomes the dominant force governing free-surface behavior, controlling how propellant settles once other forces are removed. This simulation depicts a baffled tank similar in size to the Agena Target Vehicle, where **FLOW-3D**‘s Surface Tension model captures an incoming propellant jet as it disperses and settles into its minimum-energy configuration at the tank drain.*
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Aerospace Propellant Management

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Additive Manufacturing and Laser Welding

Surface tension governs melt pool shape, bead geometry, and the wetting of molten metal on solidified substrate in both additive manufacturing and laser welding. ***FLOW-3D* AM** and ***FLOW-3D* WELD** use the surface tension model to capture melt pool dynamics, keyhole formation, and capillary penetration of liquid metal into the powder bed, giving process engineers the data they need to optimize parameters and predict defects before committing to physical trials.

**FLOW-3D AM** simulation comparing stable (left) and unstable (right) melt pool conditions in laser powder bed fusion of IN718, showing how increased scan speed at constant power drives melt pool instability and balling defects
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Additive Manufacturing and Laser Welding

text:
Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Electrowetting

By applying an electric potential across a dielectric layer, the apparent contact angle of a droplet can be modified on demand. ***FLOW-3D*** models this electrowetting effect, enabling simulation of digital microfluidic devices where droplets are steered, merged, split, and dispensed on electrode arrays without any moving parts.

**FLOW-3D** simulation of electrowetting showing a hydrophobic droplet transitioning to hydrophilic behavior under a 50V applied potential, with electric potential (top left), plan view (bottom left), and 3D electric charge density in fluid (right).
heading: Surface Tension Model > Industry Applications > Electrowetting

text:
Granular Media Model > Granular Media

Many types of granular media are encountered in processing and manufacturing industries. Because of its unusual properties, granular material can often pose difficult problems for engineers seeking to transfer, mix or otherwise manipulate it for useful purposes. The granular media model is used to predict the behavior of a mixture of solid particles and a fluid that can be either gas or liquid, e.g., sand and air or sand and water. This mixture of granular solid and fluid is treated as an incompressible fluid that may be bounded by fee surfaces. The granular media model has been developed for flows of highly concentrated granular material. The model uses a “continuum” approach, that is, it is based on a continuous fluid representation of the sand, making no attempt to treat individual sand particles.
heading: Granular Media Model > Granular Media

text:
Granular Media Model > Granular Media > Modeling Granular Media

A mixture of sand and air, is a two-phase flow in which the air and sand materials flow with their individual velocities, but are coupled through momentum exchanges resulting from pressure and viscous stresses. In typical core sands the diameters of sand particles are on the order of tenths of millimeters and the volume fraction of the sand that is blown into a cavity is generally 50% or higher. In this range a strong coupling exists between the sand and air so their mixture can be modeled as a single, composite fluid. Two-phase effects resulting from differences in the velocities of the two materials are accounted for using an approximation for their relative velocity that is referred to as a Drift-Flux.

This composite flow with a relative velocity approach has been selected as the basis for the granular media model. It is assumed that the sand/air mixture can be represented as a single fluid with a sharp free surface at its boundary with the surrounding air. The composite fluid, however, is allowed to have a non-uniform density, depending on the degree of sand compaction. The viscosity of the mixture is a function of density and shear stress. Because the majority of momentum transfer is by particle-particle collisions the sand-air mixture has the character of a shear thickening material.

For the purpose of venting pure air regions in the cavity, they are treated as adiabatic bubbles. An adiabatic bubble is a region of air surrounded by fluid or solid walls. The pressure in a bubble is a function of the bubble volume and has a uniform value over the region occupied by the bubble. Vents allow air within bubbles to be vented to the exterior of the cavity.
heading: Granular Media Model > Granular Media > Modeling Granular Media

text:
Granular Media Model > Granular Media > Granular Media Applications

To illustrate some of the differences that can occur in a granular material as opposed to a fluid, a simple two-dimensional wedge shape hopper was set up with a 1 cm wide tube at the bottom. The simulation is started with the bottom tube empty.

Sand was initialized at its close packing limit of 0.63 volume fraction. Sand at the bottom of the opening to the discharge tube begins to fall under the action of gravity, but nearly all the sand above remains stationary, Figs. 1-4, where the color is the flow resistance caused by packing (red being perfectly rigid). In a short time a bubble-like region is formed and moves up toward the top surface of the sand. Only flow around the surface of the bubble is seen until the bubble reaches the top then it causes a collapse of the surface. The indentation in the top surface has localize flow that reduces its sides to a specified angle of repose of 34°. Meanwhile another bubble forms at the bottom to repeat this pattern.

To illustrate the application of this new model, a simulation was performed to compare with data in the paper “Development and use of Simulation in the Design of Blown Cores and Moulds,” by D. Lefebvre, A. Mackenbrock, V. Vidal, V. Pavan and P.M. Haigh., Hommes & Fonderie, December 2004. The data is for a two-dimensional die geometry with one filling port. Venting of the die was asymmetric so that the influence of vents on the filling pattern could be studied.

The size of the simulation region was 30 cm wide by 15 cm high and 1 cm thick. Sand/air mixture of density 1.508 gm/cc was driven into the box with a pressure of 2 atmospheres absolute at the entrance to the box. There were five open vents on the right side of the box plus six more that were closed on the bottom and left side of the box. This arrangement leads to an asymmetric filling of the box.

The computational grid consisted of 80 mesh cells horizontally and 40 vertically. The time for the simulation to reach a fully filled core box was 0.07s and required a CPU time of about 8.9s running in serial mode on a 3.2GHz Pentium 4 PC computer (satisfyingly small, but of course, this was only a 2D case with 3200 cells in the computational region).

A comparison of the results from the continuum model simulation with photos from the Lefebvre, et al paper is given in Fig. 5. The visual agreement is seen to be very good in many details. The simulation captures the asymmetric influence of having vents closed on the left side.
heading: Granular Media Model > Granular Media > Granular Media Applications

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution

The thermal stress evolution (TSE) model in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** extends the range of casting processes that can be modeled. The FSI/TSE model describes fully-coupled interactions between fluid and solid using a finite element approach to model stresses and deformations in solid and solidified components in response to pressure forces from the surrounding fluid, thermal gradients, and specified constraints. Thermal stresses develop during the solidification process which are caused by non-uniform cooling. These stresses are influenced by shrinkage at mold walls and irregularities in the casting’s shape.

The simulation above shows the Von Mises stresses in a solidified aluminum V6 engine block. The block is composed of an Aluminum A380 alloy that was cast within a steel die. The pour temperature of the aluminum was 527°C and the initial die temperature was 125°C. The part was cooled within the die for 60s, after which the die was opened and the part continued to cool for 9 minutes in ambient conditions (125°C), totaling 10 minutes of simulation time. The von Mises stress shown is a measure of the magnitude of shear stresses within the part, thus showing regions where tearing is most like to occur. Stresses can be simultaneously computed in the mold and in the solidifying metal. Meshing can be done automatically using ***FLOW-3D***‘s structured mesh as the initial template. Users can control the local resolution of the mesh by creating nested or linked mesh blocks, and with V11.0’s new conforming mesh feature. Alternatively, users have the option of importing Finite Element meshes from third-party mesh generation software in Exodus-II format.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Simulating Thermal Stress

Shown below is an aluminum cover, also composed of Aluminum A380 alloy cast within a steel die. The pour temperature was 654°C and the initial die temperature was 240°C. The part was cooled within the die for 6s at which point the part was completely solidified (except for the runner system). The die was then opened and the part was allowed to cool a further 10s in ambient conditions (25°C). The runner system was then removed, after which a further 10s of cooling in ambient conditions occurred. The normal displacement shown here indicates the motion of the surface of the part, magnified 30 times to highlight the greatest regions of deformation.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Simulating Thermal Stress

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models

A new feature in ***FLOW-3D*** v11 is an upgrade to the existing finite-element solid mechanics solver that allows the elastic stresses between neighboring Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) components and/or the Thermal Stress Evolution (TSE) solidified fluid region to be coupled. This new capability opens the door to a wealth of modeling possibilities, including simulating thermal stresses and deformations in complex, deforming, multi-material parts (e.g., a metal casting solidifying in a mold, or bimetallic gauges), and simulating forces on connected hydraulic structures, like radial gates and pipeline support systems.

There are several different options in the model that allow for efficient computation of complex processes:
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > No coupling

This option represents the simplified case where neighboring FSI components do not exchange stresses. It is computationally efficient and is suitable for scenarios where the interaction of the stresses between components is not significant.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > No coupling

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > Full coupling

The full coupling option is for modeling neighboring FSI components that are fused together but have differing material properties. The two components cannot pull apart or slide past one another, but the stresses at the interface are transferred between the components. This is ideal for modeling bonded structures, like a bimetallic strip.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > Full coupling

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > Partial coupling

The partial coupling option is for modeling general problems where neighboring FSI components interact through frictional and normal forces but can pull apart. This option can be used to couple FSI components and the TSE solidified fluid region, making it ideal for investigating the effects of thermal stresses on a cast part and the die as the part cools in the die.

Two simulations are presented to demonstrate the new features of the model in more detail. The first situation uses the full coupling option to model a bimetallic strip bending in response to a time varying temperature, while the second example shows the use of the partial coupling model to look at thermal stresses during the solidification of a V6 engine block in a die.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Component Coupling within the Fluid-Structure Interaction and Thermal Stress Evolution Models > Partial coupling

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Full Coupling Example: Bimetallic Strip

One of the simplest examples of the full coupling option is the motion of a bimetallic strip in response to temperature gradients. Such strips are commonly used in thermal switches and bend because the two metals do not expand at the same rate in response to changes in temperature. The bimetallic strip modeled in the simulation is a cantilever beam consisting of a 15cm long, 0.5cm thick steel strip bonded to a copper strip of same dimensions, as shown in Figure 1.

The strip was then placed in an environment where the temperature was uniformly varied over 70 seconds. Figure 2 shows the deflection of the tip of the strip for the simulation and an analytical solution at various temperatures over time. The results show some interesting features, including a slight delay between when the temperature changed and the response of the strip due to the thermal inertia of the strip. This delay also influences the difference in timing between the computed and analytical deflections because the analytical solution assumed instantaneous changes in temperature. The differences in amplitude of the displacement can be attributed to the assumption of an infinitely thin strip in the analytical result. The thickness in the computational model adds additional stresses at the mounting point which leads to an increased deflection.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Full Coupling Example: Bimetallic Strip

text:
Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Partial Coupling Example: Metal Casting within a Deformable Die

The second example simulation uses the partial coupling model to show the stress development in a metal casting within a deformable steel die. The two halves of the die and the solidified fluid are partially coupled to one another, meaning that they interact through normal stresses and friction. The simulation shows the thermal stress evolution in the die and the cast part as they cool from just below the solidus temperature at 770K to the surrounding temperature of 293K. The cast part is composed of A380 aluminum alloy while the die halves are composed of H-13 steel.


The finite element mesh of the cast part and of the surrounding die is composed of 3,665,533 elements and 3,862,378 nodes, as shown in Figure 3. Also shown are the meshes, which are separate for each die half and the TSE solidified fluid region. The red circles on the front face are due to the support pistons, which are not shown.

The stresses at the interface between the mold and solidified fluid surfaces are partially coupled, and the constrained shrinkage can be seen. Figure 4 shows the resulting deformation in the cast part and one half of the die partway through the simulation. The die halves and the casting shrink at different rates as the temperature decreases, resulting in large stresses in the interfering regions and indicating potential problem areas. Computing the coupled stresses in the die and in the part allows users to better predict the stresses developing within each component and give insight into how to improve part quality and extend tool life.

The interaction of different solid objects is an important part of modern design and engineering. The addition of the new coupling options between FSI components and TSE solidified fluid regions to ***FLOW-3D*** provides a useful tool for evaluating the complex geometries regularly encountered by today’s engineers.
heading: Thermal Stress Evolution Model > Thermal Stress Evolution > Partial Coupling Example: Metal Casting within a Deformable Die

text:
Detailed Cutcell Representation

The FAVOR™ method is central to how ***FLOW-3D*** products handle complex geometry. Rather than requiring a body-fitted mesh, FAVOR™ represents solid surfaces using area and volume fractions on regular Cartesian grids, enabling efficient simulation of flow around intricate shapes without the overhead of unstructured meshing. The standard FAVOR™ treatment approximates the surface area, location, and orientation within each cutcell using just the cell area and volume fractions. This approach is efficient and sufficiently accurate for many applications, but may introduce noise in the wall shear stress and skin friction when solid surfaces cannot be aligned with the mesh planes,

The Detailed Cutcell Representation addresses this limitation by embedding a more precise geometric description of the cutcells directly into the solver. During preprocessing, the exact geometry of each cutcell is computed from a sequence of cell-plane intersections and stored alongside the standard FAVOR™ area and volume fractions. This enriched representation replaces the approximate surface relations in the discrete momentum equations, fundamentally improving the accuracy of momentum fluxes near solid boundaries. The governing equations being solved are unchanged, and the overall robustness of the solver is preserved.
heading: Detailed Cutcell Representation

text:
Detailed Cutcell Representation > When to Use Detailed Cutcell Representation

The Detailed Cutcell Representation is most beneficial when viscous boundary layer effects are important to the accuracy of the simulation and the solid geometry cannot be aligned with the mesh. Applications involving wall shear stress, skin friction, drag and lift on curved or inclined surfaces, and pressure drop in complex flow passages are the best candidates.

*Spillways are one application where accurate shear stress predictions are needed along complex surfaces. In this example, wall shear stress contours are shown for flow over an ogee spillway simulated with **FLOW-3D** **HYDRO**. Shear stress varies smoothly along the length of the spillway, despite the non-conforming, Cartesian mesh (circular inset).*
heading: Detailed Cutcell Representation > When to Use Detailed Cutcell Representation

text:
Detailed Cutcell Representation > Applications

The Detailed Cutcell Representation improves solution accuracy for a range of engineering problems where wall shear stress and boundary layer behavior matter:

- **External aerodynamics and hydrodynamics** for accurate drag, lift, and skin friction prediction on airfoils, hulls, and other streamlined bodies
- **Pipe and duct flow** for improved friction factor prediction in circular and non-rectangular cross-sections across laminar and turbulent regimes
- **Flow around inclined or curved surfaces** where geometry cannot be aligned with mesh planes and standard FAVOR™ approximations introduce noise in the shear stress field
- **Vortex shedding and wake dynamics** where accurate near-wall momentum fluxes are needed to correctly predict separation and unsteady wake behavior
heading: Detailed Cutcell Representation > Applications

text:
Mooring Lines Model

Mooring systems are central to the design and analysis of floating offshore structures, wave energy devices, and anchored marine infrastructure. ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** include a compliant Mooring Lines Model that simulates the full three-dimensional dynamics of mooring lines and their interactions with floating or moving objects. Lines can be taut or slack, may rest partially or fully on the seafloor or riverbed, and can fail under excessive load, giving engineers a realistic picture of mooring system behavior under wave, current, and structural loading conditions.
heading: Mooring Lines Model

text:
Mooring Lines Model > How the Model Works

The model uses a Finite Segment approach to compute mooring line dynamics. Each line is divided into discrete segments, and the position and velocity of each segment’s mass center are calculated by solving the dynamic equation of motion. Forces acting on each segment include gravity, buoyancy, tension at both ends, and fluid drag in the normal and tangential directions computed using a quadratic drag law.

Mooring lines can be pinned to moving. The end-point of the mooring line moves with the object. The tension of the mooring line produces forces that act on the object. This two-way coupling allows the model to capture the feedback between structural motion and line dynamics. Line endpoints can be fixed to anchors, attached to other moving or stationary objects, or defined as free ends. Multiple lines can be present in a single simulation with an arbitrary connection configurations.

The mooring line model can be used for even when the line extends below the computational domain, as is common when anchoring to deep water seafloors. The submerged portion of the line outside the domain is treated with a uniform deep-water current assumption and drag forces are evaluated accordingly.

Line failure is also supported. At each time step the maximum tension in each line segment is compared against a user-defined Minimum Breaking Load, and the line severs at the point of maximum tension if that threshold is exceeded.

*A floating structure restrained by four mooring lines anchored to the seabed. Mooring line extension from free state (top right) and vertical velocity of the structure center of mass (bottom right) are shown alongside the 3D simulation.*
heading: Mooring Lines Model > How the Model Works

text:
Mooring Lines Model > Applications

The Mooring Lines Model addresses a wide range of offshore and marine engineering applications:

- **Floating Production Storage and Offloading (FPSO) vessels** for analyzing mooring system response to wave and current loading in offshore oil and gas operations
- **Wave energy converters (WECs)** for simulating how mooring configurations affect device motion, power capture, and structural loads
- **Floating wave breakers** for evaluating mooring forces and breakwater performance under design wave conditions
- **Anchored ships** **and marine vessels** for assessing mooring line loads and vessel motion in port or offshore environments
- **Floating infrastructure and equipment** for modeling buoys, platforms, pontoons, and other moored structures subject to hydrodynamic loading

*Wave action drives the displacement of a moored buoy, with mooring line tension and extension tracked throughout the simulation alongside the overall displacement of the floating structure.*
heading: Mooring Lines Model > Applications

text:
Clarifier Settling Model

In primary and secondary wastewater treatment, sludge must be separated from the water column efficiently for the treatment process to work. The settling behavior of sludge varies with local concentration gradients, the velocity of the surrounding fluid, and the gravitational settling characteristics of the sludge itself. Clarifier settling behavior and efficiency affects everything from tank residence time and effluent quality to aeration demand and overall plant capacity.

The Clarifier Settling Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulates the transport and settling of sludge in septic tanks, clarifiers, secondary settling tanks, and other wastewater treatment equipment. It accounts for the three-way interaction between gravitational settling, advection with the water flow, and diffusion, giving engineers a spatially resolved picture of how sludge distributes and settles through the treatment process.

*Sludge concentration (kg/m3) in a two-chamber settling tank at t = 160 seconds, showing accumulation at the bottom of the primary chamber and early settlement in the secondary chamber.*
heading: Clarifier Settling Model

text:
Clarifier Settling Model > How the Model Works

Sludge is treated as a scalar quantity transported within the water-sludge mixture. Its motion is governed by three components: advection with the bulk fluid, and gravitational settling, and diffusion. The settling velocity is a function of the local sludge mass concentration – as concentration increases, settling slows due to particle-particle interactions, until a maximum settled concentration is reached. At that threshold, settling stops entirely, avoiding over-concentration of settled sludge, although the sludge can still be advected by the fluid. Diffusion accounts for both the molecular diffusion of the suspended sludge in water and turbulent diffusion.

Two methods are available for defining the settling velocity as a function of concentration. The Vesilind equation uses two calibrated parameters – maximum settling velocity and a concentration decay parameter – to describe the settling rate across the full concentration range. Alternatively, the relationship can be defined directly from laboratory settling test data as a tabular function, giving engineers full flexibility when measured data is available.
heading: Clarifier Settling Model > How the Model Works

text:
Clarifier Settling Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Clarifier Settling Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** computes:

- Spatial distribution of sludge mass concentration throughout the tank at every time step
- Settling velocity as a function of local sludge concentration, using either the Vesilind equation or a user-defined tabular function
- Advection of sludge with the bulk water-sludge mixture velocity
- Turbulent and molecular diffusion of sludge within the flow field
- As settled sludge reaches a concentration threshold, the thickness of the settled sludge layer increases. Settled sludge is still advected by the fluid
- Suspended sludge at inflow boundaries, is defined as a constant or time-varying concentration
- Total sludge mass as a history output for monitoring sludge accumulation over time
- Sludge mass concentration, settling velocity, and settling mass flux as spatial outputs for postprocessing
heading: Clarifier Settling Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Clarifier Settling Model > Applications

The Clarifier Settling Model is used in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** for:

- Predicting sludge accumulation zones in primary and secondary clarifiers to optimize tank geometry and baffle placement
- Evaluating the effect of inlet flow rate and sludge loading on settling performance and effluent quality
- Evaluating sludge flushing efficiency
- Assessing short-circuiting in settling tanks where flow bypasses the intended settling zone
- Designing and optimizing septic tanks, Imhoff tanks, and other decentralized wastewater treatment systems
- Investigating the resuspension of settled sludge during flow surges or peak loading events
- Supporting regulatory compliance assessments by predicting settled sludge volumes and effluent concentrations
heading: Clarifier Settling Model > Applications

text:
Tailings Model

Tailings dam failures are among the most catastrophic events in the mining industry. When a dam fails, a flood of hyper-concentrated slurry of water and mine waste can flow with tremendous force across large distances, causing loss of life, infrastructure damage, and severe environmental harm. Understanding the runout, including how fast, how deep, and how far the inundation will reach. Understanding the flow behavior is central to risk assessment andemergency planning.

The Tailings Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulates flows with a non-Newtonian rheology. It treats tailings as a two-species system of fine and coarse particles suspended in water, each with its own concentration, density, settling behavior, and contribution to the mixture viscosity. The shear-thinning behavior of a tailings slurry is captured using a bimodal viscosity model based on the Herschel-Bulkley framework, allowing accurate prediction of flow runout distance, inundation area, and arrival times at downstream locations.

*Tailings dam breach simulated using a hybrid 2D/3D mesh in **FLOW-3D HYDRO**. Fine tailings concentration is shown as the flood spreads across the downstream terrain. The 3D mesh near the breach captures layered tailings with varied concentration and the ensuing vertical mixing; the 2D shallow water mesh covers the larger runout area efficiently.*
heading: Tailings Model

text:
Tailings Model > How the Model Works

Tailings are modeled as a mixture of two particle species: fine particles and coarse particles, separated by a grain size threshold. Each species is transported independently within the flow, governed by advection, diffusion, and settling driven deposition. The mixture density and viscosity are computed in every cell from the local concentrations of each species, so the flow resistance and runout behavior respond dynamically as the mixture evolves.
heading: Tailings Model > How the Model Works

text:
Tailings Model > How the Model Works > Bimodal Viscosity Model

The viscosity of a tailings mixture depends on both the fine and coarse particle fractions and their interaction. Fine particles form a colloidal suspension whose rheology is governed by interparticle forces: at low concentrations the suspension behaves nearly as a Newtonian fluid, but as concentration increases, particle-particle interactions dominate and the mixture becomes strongly non-Newtonian, with a measurable yield stress and shear-thinning behavior. The fluid’s rheology is modeled using the Herschel-Bulkley model, where the Herchel-Bulkley parameters, yield stress, consistency, and flow index, all varying with local concentration.

Coarse particles do not directly contribute to the yield stress of the fluid, but at high coarse fractions they significantly increase the overall mixture viscosity. The bimodal viscosity model accounts for this by computing the fluid rheology from the fine particle concentration, then applying a coarse-fraction correction to the Herschel-Bulkley’s yield stress and consistency parameters.

Three empirical correlation approaches are available for defining the effect of coarse particles on viscosity: the distance ratio model, the Thomas correlation, and the Ovarlez model. Alternatively, the rheological parameters can be specified directly from laboratory measurements using tabular data, giving engineers full flexibility to match the model to site-specific tailings behavior.
heading: Tailings Model > How the Model Works > Bimodal Viscosity Model

text:
Tailings Model > How the Model Works > Particle Species

Fine and coarse particle species can be activated independently or together:

- Fine particles form a colloidal suspension with the fluid. Their rheological parameters can be defined by tabulated data or empirical correlations fitted to laboratory measurements of the specific tailings material.
- Coarse particles are transported by the flow and settle under gravity. Their settling velocity can be defined by tabulated data or computed from standard correlations.
- When both species are active, the fine particle suspension acts as the carrier fluid for the coarse particles, and the mixture viscosity reflects the combined contribution of both fractions.
- Simulations can include Newtonian fluid behavior for areas with low particle concentrations, such as a supernatant water layer above the tailings layers or a river that the tailings breach flows into.
heading: Tailings Model > How the Model Works > Particle Species

text:
Tailings Model > Meshing Approaches

Tailings dam failures and other non-Newtonain flows often span hundreds to kilometers, but the details of the breach and early flow are localized and three-dimensional. ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO**‘s hybrid meshing framework allows engineers to match the mesh type to the flow’s modeling requirements in each part of the domain.

- 3D meshing captures the three-dimensional flow structures within the dam and in the near-field immediately downstream of the breach, including mixing, settling, and vertical concentration gradients within the tailings flow.
- Shallow water meshing provides fast, efficient solutions over the large downstream runout area where the flow is fully mixed and the depth-averaged approximation is valid.
- Hybrid 3D/shallow water meshing couples both approaches in a single simulation, allowing 3D resolution of the dam breach and early flow with shallow water efficiency for the far-field runout.
heading: Tailings Model > Meshing Approaches

text:
Tailings Model > Validation: Brumadinho, Brazil (2019)

On January 25th, 2019, the Corrego do Feijao tailings dam at Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, Brazil, failed catastrophically. The failure resulted in significant loss of life and is one of the most extensively documented tailings dam failures in recent history. The construction materials, dam geometry, and the times at which the tailings flow reached key downstream locations are all well documented, making it an ideal validation case.

The ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulation used the documented dam geometry and tailings properties. The simulated runout compares closely with observed inundation extents and arrival times at three key downstream locations: the site canteen, the railway bridge, and the Paraopeba River.

| Location | Observed time of arrival | Simulated time of arrival | 
|---|---|---|
| Canteen | 2 minutes | 2 minutes 10 seconds | 
| Railway bridge | 10 to 12 minutes | 9 minutes 30 seconds | 
| Paraopeba River | 1 hr 30 min to 2 hr 10 min | 2 hrs 18 minutes | 

[1] Lumbroso, D., Davison, M., Body, R., and Petkovšek, G.: *Modelling the Brumadinho tailings dam failure, the subsequent loss of life and how it could have been reduced*, Nat. Hazards Earth Syst. Sci., 21, 21–37, 2021. https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-21-21-2021
heading: Tailings Model > Validation: Brumadinho, Brazil (2019)

Sensitivity studies like this provide a guide to model uncertainty and help quantify the effect of rheological parameter variation on runout predictions.*

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions

Accurately representing wave boundary conditions is fundamental to simulating coastal and offshore engineering problems. Whether modeling wave forces on a structure, wave break performance, wave overtopping of a seawall, wave-induced scour around a foundation, or the performance of a wave energy converter, the wave boundary condition determines the quality of everything downstream.

***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** support a comprehensive set of wave generation methods covering regular and irregular waves across the full range of water depths, from deep water offshore to shallow coastal and nearshore environments. Waves are generated directly at mesh block boundaries and propagate through the computational. The defined wave profile at the boundary can also be applied as an initial condition to the computational domain. 

*Wave forces acting on a coastal walkway and flood wall, with hydrodynamic force on the wall object exported directly for structural analysis.*
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Linear Waves

Linear waves have a sinusoidal surface profile with small amplitude relative to the wavelength and water depth. They are generated using Airy linear wave theory and are appropriate for open-ocean conditions where wave steepness is low. An irregular wave can also be defined by superposing up to 1000 linear component waves with independent frequencies, amplitudes, and phase shifts, allowing arbitrary wave spectra to be represented without using a standard spectral formulation.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Linear Waves

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Stokes Waves

Stokes waves are nonlinear periodic waves appropriate for deep and intermediate water depths. They have sharper crests and flatter troughs than linear waves of the same height and period. Two generation methods are available: Fenton’s Fourier series method and Fenton’s fifth-order theory.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Stokes Waves

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Cnoidal Waves

Cnoidal waves are nonlinear periodic waves appropriate for shallow and intermediate water depths. They are more peaked and asymmetric than Stokes waves of equivalent energy and are generated using Fenton’s Fourier series method. Fenton’s method is valid across the full range of periodic wave types from deep to shallow water.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Cnoidal Waves

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Solitary Waves

A solitary wave is a single, non-periodic wave that exists entirely above the undisturbed water level. It is the limiting form of a cnoidal wave as wavelength approaches infinity and is relevant for modeling tsunami-like events, dam breaks, and large impulsive wave loading on coastal structures. Solitary waves are generated using McCowan’s theory.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Solitary Waves

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Irregular Waves

***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** generate irregular waves using the Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum, which describes fully developed windy seas, or the JONSWAP spectrum, which accounts for fetch-limited growth in coastal and semi-enclosed environments. A user-defined spectrum can also be imported from an external file for site-specific sea state representation.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Types > Irregular Waves

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Generation Options

Wave conditions in ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** can be specified:

- As a boundary condition at any of the four horizontal mesh block faces (X min, X max, Y min, Y max), where the wave enters the domain and propagates inward
- As an initial condition throughout the fluid domain, which initializes the wave field everywhere simultaneously and avoids the transient startup period needed for waves generated at a boundary to fill the domain
- With a superimposed steady current at the wave boundary, allowing combined wave-current conditions to be represented
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Generation Options

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Applicability Chart

Selecting the appropriate wave theory for a given set of conditions depends on the wave height, wave period, and water depth. ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** include a wave applicability chart based on established coastal engineering guidance to help users identify the correct wave generator for their application. Fenton’s Fourier series method is valid across the full range of periodic wave conditions and is the recommended default for all regular wave types.
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Wave Applicability Chart

text:
Wave Boundary Conditions > Applications

Waves Boundary Conditions are used in ***FLOW-3D*** and ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** for:

- Wave force and overtopping analysis for coastal protection structures, seawalls, and breakwaters
- Wave transmission and reflection across breakwater structures
- Wave-structure interaction for offshore platforms, gravity-based structures, and subsea foundations
- Wave energy converter design and performance assessment
- Tsunami and extreme wave loading on coastal infrastructure
- Nearshore wave transformation including shoaling, refraction, and breaking over complex bathymetry
- Wave-induced scour and sediment transport around coastal and offshore structures
- Harbor resonance and wave penetration analysis
- Wave interaction with floating and moored structures, in combination with the moving object and mooring lines models

*Wave attenuation by a living shoreline reef structure, showing flow depth and a 65% reduction in wave height after passing through the WAD® reef elements.*
heading: Wave Boundary Conditions > Applications

text:
Hydraulic Boundary Conditions

Boundary conditions, where flow enters or exits a model domain, can have a consequential impact on the calculated flow field and if it accurately simulates the real-world condition. A river reach for example, extends beyond the model domain. –The domain downstream of the model usually influences the water surface elevation at the downstream end of the model. The velocity distribution entering the model is usually the result of river geometry beyond the domain. Specifying these boundaries correctly is necessary for the model to produce accurate water surface profiles, capture hydraulic jumps and backwater effects, and respond realistically to flood wave propagation.

***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** includes a set of hydraulic boundary conditions designed for open channel, river and coastal modeling that incorporate waves, rating curves, natural inlet treatments, mass sources, and flow regime controls that hydraulic engineers work with in practice.
heading: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions

text:
Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Rating Curve Boundary Condition

A rating curve describes the relationship between water surface elevation and discharge at a river cross-section. Rating curves are the standard tool for characterizing flow conditions at downstream model boundaries. Rating curves can be measured in the field when possible or calculated from a calibrated river model, such as HEC-RAS.

In transient ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** models, rating curve boundary conditions can be applied at both inlet and outlet boundaries. At an inlet, the rating curve defines the inflowing water surface elevation and the model flow is an artifact of the model geometry and associated headloss. At an outlet, the rating curve provides a physically consistent downstream water surface elevation that responds to the simulated discharge or time. Allowing the water surface to vary with flow eliminates the need for a fixed pressure boundary that may not reflect actual downstream conditions.

*Rating curve boundary condition example showing a flood wave simulation. Time histories of fluid elevation and volume flow rate at the inlet (xmin) and outlet (xmax) boundaries are shown alongside the Froude number distribution along the channel. The inlet rating curve forces a supercritical flood wave; the outlet uses a subcritical rating curve, producing a hydraulic jump in the domain.*
heading: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Rating Curve Boundary Condition

text:
Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Volume Flow Rate Boundary Condition

At an inlet where only the flow is known and no water surface elevation data is available, the Volume Flow Rate boundary condition allows the inflow depth to vary with conditions (regime) at the boundary of the domain. A minimum and maximum fluid elevations can be provided, to limit water level range and prevent inadvertent super-critical flow when subcritical conditions are expected.

The shallow water volume flow rate boundary condition offers a spatially varying velocity profile at the inlet. This reduces the need for additional upstream domain length to allow the flow profile to develop before reaching the area of interest. Users can choose between a uniform, parabolic and depth-depending velocity profiles. The last option is particularly useful for river applications where the velocity is high in deep water and low at shallow water. A user defined lateral velocity variation is not available.

*The same flood wave scenario with the inlet changed to a subcritical volume flow rate boundary condition. Without supercritical forcing at the inlet, the domain maintains subcritical flow throughout, as shown by the lower Froude numbers across the channel.*
heading: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Volume Flow Rate Boundary Condition

text:
Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Natural Inlet Boundary Condition

For natural channels where neither rating curve data nor a fixed water surface elevation is available, the Natural Inlet boundary condition sets the water depth at the inlet using the depth in the adjacent cells immediately inside the domain and/or the depth in the previous time step. This eliminates the potential for sharp discontinuities in water surface elevation at the inlet that could cause numeric instabilities in transient simulations.

As the water surface inside the domain rises or falls in response to changing flow conditions, the inlet adjusts automatically to match. The flow regime at a natural inlet can be specified as subcritical, supercritical, critical, or automatic – where the automatic option allows the flow category to change during the simulation based on computed Froude number. Minimum and maximum elevation limits can also be set to prevent the inlet water surface from dropping below terrain level or exceeding a physical upper bound.

A rating curve relaxation time option is available for natural inlet boundary conditions, to improve the response to transient flow conditions and reduce numerical oscillations when the inlet flow rate changes rapidly.
heading: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Natural Inlet Boundary Condition

text:
Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Applications

Hydraulic boundary conditions in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** are required for all simulations but are notable for their ability to include the following cases:

- Flood wave propagation modeling for hydraulic structures in 3D and shallow water model
- River reach simulations where time dependent upstream and downstream gauge data is available as rating curves
- Models where discharge is known but stage data is unavailable
- Hydraulic jump and backwater analysis where accurate downstream boundary conditions are critical
- Inlet boundary setup for models where flow profile development length would otherwise require a large upstream domain
- Time-varying flood scenarios where inlet discharge follows a hydrograph and outlet conditions respond dynamically
heading: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions > Applications

text:
Contact Line Pinning Model

A contact line is the boundary, where liquid free surface meets solid substrate. In many real-world situations, this line does not slide freely along the surface but instead pins to a fixed position, remaining stationary while the shape of the liquid above it changes.

This behavior is often observed on rough, contaminated or otherwise imperfect surfaces or due to coating. A familiar example is a coffee ring stain: as a spilled coffee droplet gradually evaporates over time, the shape of the droplet on the table largely remains unchanged, resulting in a concentrated ring of residue. Similar processes are responsible for water droplets getting stuck on a windshield. Away from the natural environment, specially engineered surfaces are used in the controlled deposition of inkjet droplets and the management of liquid films in microfluidic devices. ***FLOW-3D*** includes a contact line pinning model that enables simulation of this behavior in surface-tension-dominated flows.

*A liquid aluminum alloy droplet impacts a surface with two wetting conditions: a static contact angle of 40° on the gray surface and a pinned contact line on the orange surface, showing droplet distortion and jetting at the interface between the two regions.*
heading: Contact Line Pinning Model

text:
Contact Line Pinning Model > How It Works

The contact line pinning model works in conjunction with surface tension model and is applied as a property of geometry surfaces. When a fluid contact line encounters a solid surface marked with the pinning attribute, it becomes anchored at that location.

The pinning is enforced by setting the outward velocity of the fluid at the contact point to zero, preventing the contact line from advancing along the surface. Fluid can recede from the original contact location due to evaporation. It can also roll over the pinning point if more fluid is added to the area, but the contact line cannot slide as it would at regular geometry surfaces.

Flow near a pinned contact line is a result of the balance of forces, including surface tension forces arising from the specified static contact angle, viscous forces and gravity.

The contact line pinning model can be used together with the vaporization residue model when simulating evaporative deposition, tracking the accumulation and spreading of solid residue on the substrate.
heading: Contact Line Pinning Model > How It Works

text:
Contact Line Pinning Model > Applications

The contact line pinning model extends the surface tension and wetting capabilities of ***FLOW-3D*** to a broader range of surface-tension-dominated problems:

- **Inkjet printing** for predicting droplet spreading, contact line behavior, and residue deposition patterns on substrates
- **Spray and evaporative cooling** for modeling the behavior of droplets on heated surfaces, where contact line dynamics influence heat transfer rates
- **Coating and film deposition** for simulating the behavior of liquid films on engineered surfaces, where wetting control is important
- **Microfluidic devices** for modeling liquid sample movement in channels and chambers, where surface engineering controls wetting and pinning behavior
- **Evaporative deposition and residue formation** for predicting the location and concentration of solid residue left behind as liquid evaporates from a pinned droplet
heading: Contact Line Pinning Model > Applications

text:
Sediment Transport Model

Accurately predicting sediment transport from bedload movement to suspended sediment concentration, erosion and deposition, is critical to designing hydraulic structures that perform reliably over their operational life. Yet it remains difficult to model with confidence, particularly where flow fields are highly three-dimensional, as in water intakes, stormwater separators, reservoir flushing and others. In these applications, sediment transport must be incorporated into the CFD simulation and cannot be simplified through depth-averaged approximations.

The Sediment Transport Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulates bedload and suspended sediment transport, erosion, and deposition for non-cohesive sediment. The model is fully coupled to the hydrodynamic solver, so the evolving bed geometry feeds back into the flow field at every time step. Up to 10 different sediment species can be defined simultaneously, each with its own grain size, density, critical shear stress, angle of repose, and transport parameters, allowing realistic representation of graded sediment mixtures.

*Stormwater sediment basin simulated in **FLOW-3D HYDRO**, showing scalar flow patterns (left), suspended sediment concentration (center), sediment depth accumulation on the basin floor (upper right), and cross-sectional velocity (lower right). As sediment settles and deposits, the solid geometry updates within the model in real time.*
heading: Sediment Transport Model

text:
Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works

In ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO**, sediment exists in two states: a packed bed, represented by the FAVOR™ method as an erodible solid boundary, and  as suspended sediment, represented as a scalar mass concentration transported with the fluid. The exchange between these two states is computed at every cell containing the bed interface.
heading: Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works

text:
Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works > Bedload Transport

Bedload transport is the movement of sediment grains rolling, sliding and saltating along the channel bed without entering full suspension. In ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO**, the volumetric bedload transport rate per unit width is computed using one of three well-established empirical equations: Meyer-Peter and Muller (1948) for gravel beds, Van Rijn (1984) for sand beds, and Nielsen (1992) for coastal wave environments. Bed shear stress is evaluated using the law of the wall, with bed roughness proportional to the local median grain diameter.
heading: Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works > Bedload Transport

text:
Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works > Entrainment and Suspension

Entrainment is the process by which turbulent eddies lift grains from the packed bed surface and carry them into suspension. The entrainment rate is based on the local Shields parameter relative to the critical value for that grain size. The critical Shields parameter can be computed automatically or specified directly and is adjusted for sloping bed surfaces using the angle of repose.

Particle-particle interactions at higher sediment concentrations are accounted for in the settling velocity calculation. The relative rates of entrainment and settling control the exchange of sediment mass between the packed bed and suspended states.
heading: Sediment Transport Model > How the Model Works > Entrainment and Suspension

text:
Sediment Transport Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Sediment Transport Model in ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** supports:

- Unsteady 3D mobile bed modeling fully coupled to the hydrodynamic solver
- Bedload transport using Meyer-Peter and Muller, Van Rijn or Nielsen equations
- Suspended sediment transport, entrainment, and deposition for non-cohesive sediments
- Up to 10 simultaneous sediment species with independent grain size, density, critical shear stress, and angle of repose
- Slope-adjusted entrainment thresholds based on angle of repose
- Compatible with both 3D and shallow water mesh configurations
heading: Sediment Transport Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Sediment Transport Model > Applications

Simulations like this support dam safety assessment by quantifying scour depth and lateral extent under design flood conditions.*
