text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model

Standard CFD models treat fluids as purely viscous, whereas many complex materials exhibit time-dependent viscoelastic constitutive behaviors, where stress response depends on both the instantaneous shear rate and the deformation history. Polymer melts resist rapid deformation like a solid yet flow easily under slow shear. Filled suspensions like cement, food products, or slurries behave rigidly up to a stress threshold, then yield and flow. Accurately simulating these materials requires models that capture both the viscous and elastic contributions to stress, and their interaction over time.

***FLOW-3D*** provides a family of models for non-Newtonian fluids with elastic behavior, covering both viscoelastic materials, where viscous and elastic stresses interact continuously, and elasto-viscoplastic materials, where the material transitions from solid-like to liquid-like behavior when a yield stress is exceeded.
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models

Viscoelasticity can be well explained with the classic oscillatory shear experiment simulated below with ***FLOW-3D***. A rectangular fluid element is placed between two plates. The top plate moves with a sinusoidal velocity, and the horizontal force is measured at the bottom plate. We can observe that the maximum force for a Newtonian fluid is measured when the top plate velocity is maximum when the shear rate is the highest. For purely elastic material (such as solid), the maximum force is in the most pivoted position of the top plate, i.e. when the displacement (or strain) is the highest. Viscoelastic fluid response is a mixture of those two ideal fluids, when both viscosity and elasticity play a role for the overall rheological response.

Viscoelastic materials exhibit time-dependent mechanical behavior: they respond like an elastic solid under rapid deformation and like a viscous liquid under slow deformation. The classic example is a polymer melt or solution, where long molecular chains become entangled under rapid shear and resist deformation, but slide past each other easily under slow flow. The relative contribution of viscous and elastic stress changes continuously depending on the local strain rate.

Two built-in viscoelastic constitutive models are available in ***FLOW-3D***:
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Oldroyd-B Model

The Oldroyd-B model is the simplest viscoelastic model and is appropriate for dilute polymer solutions. It represents the polymer contribution to stress as a Hookean spring in series with a dashpot, producing a fluid that has a constant viscosity but exhibits elastic stress that decays exponentially after flow stops. It is a good starting point for viscoelastic flow problems where material data is limited. The Oldroyd-B model is suited for viscoelastic flows with a low Weissenberg number, that is when the characteristic strain rate is lower than the reciprocal of the relaxation time.
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Oldroyd-B Model

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Giesekus Model

**. For comparison, Newtonian and Giesekus rheology models were used. We can see that the viscoelastic fluid displays a plug-like flow inside the nozzle and yields uneven bead shape after the deposition, compared to a smooth surface of the Newtonian fluid. This is an important effect for processes such as fused deposition modelling or robocasting.**

*FLOW-3D*
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Giesekus Model

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Custom Viscoelastic Models

For materials that do not fit either built-in model, ***FLOW-3D*** supports custom viscoelastic constitutive equations through a user-modifiable Fortran routine. This allows additional terms to be added to the elastic stress formulation without modifying the core solver.
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Viscoelastic Models > Custom Viscoelastic Models

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Elasto-Viscoplastic Materials

Elasto-viscoplastic materials behave as elastic solids up to a yield stress threshold, beyond which they flow as viscous fluids. This behavior describes a wide range of industrially important materials including fresh concrete, food products, muds, and highly filled suspensions such as toothpaste or solder paste. Below the yield stress, the material stores energy elastically and deforms without flowing. Above it, the material yields and flows with plastic deformation.

The elasto-viscoplastic model in ***FLOW-3D*** uses an incremental Hookean elastic stress formulation, computing the change in elastic stress from one time step to the next based on the local incremental strain. Because each increment is computed over a small time step where the deformation is small, the model can accurately predict large, highly nonlinear deformations over long time scales. Temperature-dependent elastic shear modulus and yield stress can be specified using tabular data when the Heat Transfer model is active.
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Elasto-Viscoplastic Materials

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Constitutive Law Formulations

For both the Oldroyd-B and Giesekus viscoelastic models, two formulations of the constitutive law are available:

- Stress tensor formulation: solves for the elastic stress tensor. Lower computational cost per time step, appropriate for low Weissenberg number flows.
- Log-conformation tensor formulation: solves for the logarithm of the conformation tensor, which is a representation of elastic strain, rather than the stress tensor directly. This formulation is more robust in high Weissenberg number flows, where the stress tensor formulation can develop numerical instabilities. Recommended when elastic stress is large relative to viscous stress.

The simulation below is a classic case of 4:1 contraction flow that features a sharp corner. While the stress tensor formulation becomes unstable after 3s of the flow due to exponential growth of the elastic stress, log-conformation tensor formulation remain stable and enables robust simulation.

The log-conformation tensor formulation is a significant improvement for demanding polymer flow simulations, such as high-speed injection molding, extrusion through sharp dies, and other flows where elastic stress dominates.
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Constitutive Law Formulations

text:
Viscoelastic Flow Model > Applications

The Viscoelastic Flow Model in ***FLOW-3D*** is used for:

- Polymer melt injection molding: predicting fill patterns, weld line locations, and die swell effects that viscous models cannot capture
- Extrusion die design: modeling extrudate swell and flow instabilities in profile and film extrusion
- Food processing: simulating flow of non-Newtonian food products including doughs, gels, and emulsions
- Cement and concrete placement: predicting flow and self-leveling behavior of fresh concrete and grout
- Pharmaceutical manufacturing: modeling filled suspensions, ointments, and other yield-stress formulations
- Solder paste printing and dispensing in electronics manufacturing
- Biofluid mechanics: simulating blood and other biological fluids with viscoelastic rheology
heading: Viscoelastic Flow Model > Applications

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model

Tracking discrete particles through a fluid flow opens up a broad class of engineering problems that cannot be addressed with fluid-only simulations. ***FLOW-3D*** products include a Lagrangian Particle Model that tracks individual particles as they move through the fluid domain, exchanging momentum, heat, mass, and electric charge with the surrounding flow. Particles can represent solid grains, liquid droplets, gas bubbles, massless tracers, and more, and can interact with each other, with the fluid, and with solid geometry in the same coupled simulation.
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Particle Classes

Seven particle classes are available, each representing a distinct physical type or function:

- **Mass particles** are solid spheres with user-defined density and diameter, such as dust, sand, powder, inclusions, or other solid particulates.
- **Fluid particles** are liquid droplets whose physical properties match the primary fluid. They can be used to model sprays, atomization, and droplet-laden flows. Fluid particles can solidify and re-melt, and can evaporate and condense when the two-fluid phase change model is active.
- **Gas particles** are compressible bubbles governed by the ideal gas equation of state, whose size changes dynamically with local temperature and pressure. When a gas particle escapes the free surface, it adds its volume to the surrounding gas region. The underlying bubble and phase change model has been reorganized and simplified, consolidating the adiabatic and thermal bubble models into a single ideal gas equation of.
- **Void particles** are a specialized class used to track collapsed bubble regions, making them useful for identifying potential porosity defects in casting and other processes.
- **Probe particles** are diagnostic particles that record and report flow variable values at their location. They can be stationary or moving and can be of any other particle class.
- **Marker particles** are massless tracers with no physical properties, used to visualize flow patterns and track fluid pathlines.
- **User particles** are up to ten fully customizable classes defined through user-defined functions, each carrying three configurable attributes.

Each material particle class (mass, fluid, gas, user) supports multiple species of different sizes and densities within the same simulation. A macro-coefficient option allows a single simulated particle to represent a cloud of identical physical particles, reducing computational cost in regions of high concentration without sacrificing accuracy.

*VOF to Particles: Small fluid droplets generated at the point of impact are automatically converted from VOF representation to fluid particles, improving mass and momentum conservation in regions subject to breakup.*

The VOF-to-Particles capability is available across the product family. Small fluid ligaments and droplets that are difficult to track accurately with the VOF method are automatically converted to fluid particles when certain conditions are met. Particle motion is then handled by the Lagrangian Particle Model, and particles are converted back to VOF representation when they reenter the fluid. This improves mass and momentum conservation for fluid regions subject to breakup and can allow higher time steps in many simulations..

The Lagrangian Particle Model interface in ***FLOW-3D* CAST** provides a streamlined setup experience for casting-specific particle workflows.
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Particle Classes

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Particle Physics and Coupling

The motion of each particle is governed by Newton’s second law. Forces acting on a particle include gravity, pressure (buoyancy), drag, and added-mass. The particle drag coefficient is computed as a function of the local particle Reynolds number and particle concentration. Heat transfer between particles and the surrounding fluid is available for all material particle classes, enabling thermal equilibration, melting and solidification, and droplet evaporation to be captured within the simulation.

By default, particle motion is influenced by the fluid but has no effect on it. When two-way coupling is enabled, momentum exchange between particles and fluid is solved implicitly, capturing the feedback from the particles on the surrounding fluid field. This is important in applications where particle concentrations or masses are significant enough to alter the flow field.
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Particle Physics and Coupling

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Discrete Element Method (DEM)

The Discrete Element Method is an extension of the Lagrangian Particle Model that applies to solid (mass and solidified fluid) particles. When enabled, DEM adds particle-particle collision and friction physics to the simulation, resolving normal, tangential, and rotational contact forces between particles and between particles and solid geometry. Particles using DEM can also displace fluid volume as they move, an important effect for coupled fluid-particle flows with moderate to high particle concentrations.

DEM is well suited to applications where the physical interactions between individual solid particles matter, such as granular flow in hoppers and separators, rock stability assessment on riverbanks, and stormwater grit separation. In applications where particle concentrations are low or particle-particle contacts are infrequent, the standard particle model without DEM is typically sufficient and computationally less expensive.

*DEM Grit Separator: Solid particles are tracked through a cyclonic separator using the DEM model, capturing particle-particle and particle-wall interactions to evaluate separation efficiency and system performance.*

heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Discrete Element Method (DEM)

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications

The Lagrangian Particle Model supports a wide range of applications across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family:

- **Spray and atomization** for tracking droplet formation, transport, and impact in coating, cooling, and combustion processes
- **Powder and particle transport** for modeling solid particles through process equipment including mixers, fluidized beds, classifiers, and conveyors
- **Bubble dynamics** for simulating gas bubble motion, growth, and collapse in bubble column reactors, degassing systems, and cavitating flows
- **Additive manufacturing** for tracking metal powder particles through melt pool dynamics in laser powder bed fusion and directed metal deposition processes
- **Inclusion tracking in casting** for following non-metallic inclusions or porosity-forming bubbles through filling and solidification to identify defect locations
- **Granular flow and particle separation** for simulating dense solid particle flows in hoppers, separators, and channel protection systems using DEM
- **Pollutant and sediment tracking** for following suspended particles through water and environmental flows to assess transport, deposition, and separation
- **Flow visualization and diagnostics** for seeding marker or probe particles to reveal flow structures, recirculation zones, and residence time distributions
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications > Application Example: Metal Powder Bed Fusion

In laser powder bed fusion, a laser scans across a bed of metal powder particles, selectively melting and fusing them to build up a solid layer. ***FLOW-3D* AM** simulates this process using a two-stage simulation approach:

1. The particles model with DEM is used to simulate solidified metal particles settling under gravity, to generate a powder bed.
2. The settled particles are converted to a solidified fluid, which are heated/melted/re-solidified by one or more laser heat sources.

The example below shows the melting of stainless steel 316 particles on a copper substrate, with velocity vectors in the melt pool and temperature field of the solidified track shown alongside the 3D powder bed geometry.

*Melting Stainless Steel 316 Particles simulated in FLOW-3D AM. Top: 3D view of the powder bed with velocity vectors in the melt pool. Bottom left: Temperature field of the solidified track. Bottom right: track geometry after solidification.*
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications > Application Example: Metal Powder Bed Fusion

text:
Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications > Application Example: Produced Water Separator

Produced water separators must reliably separate oil, water, and gas while also managing entrained sand, across a range of flow rates and inlet conditions, behavior that is difficult to predict with hand calculations alone. ***FLOW-3D* HYDRO** simulates the internal hydraulics of a 3-phase separator, capturing flow through a perforated baffle, sand baffle, vortex breakers, and spillover weir. The oil phase is modeled using the Dispersed Multiphase Model, while sand is tracked using Mass Particles within the Lagrangian Particle Model, allowing sand settling and accumulation along the vessel floor to be resolved alongside the oil-water separation.

*3-phase separation of oil, water, and sand simulated in **FLOW-3D HYDRO**, showing internal hydraulics through a perforated baffle, sand baffle, vortex breakers, and spillover weir as the phases stratify and sand settles along the vessel floor.*
heading: Lagrangian Particle Model > Applications > Application Example: Produced Water Separator

text:
Heat Transfer Model

Heat transfer plays a significant role across a wide range of engineering applications. The change in temperature governs a material’s properties and determines how and when it changes phase. In hydraulic flows, this results in the buoyant motion of a thermal plume ejecting into a river or the freezing of a storage tank in winter. For metal casting, additive manufacturing, and welding, proper management of the transfer of heat determines how and where defects form and the thermal loads present.

The ***FLOW-3D*** product family accounts for the conduction, convection, and radiation within and between all three phases (fluid, solid, and void/gas) by solving the full conjugate heat transfer equations. The Heat Transfer Model forms the thermal foundation on which phase change, solidification, die cycling, spray cooling, and thermal stress models all depend.
heading: Heat Transfer Model

text:
Heat Transfer Model > Modeling Capabilities

The Heat Transfer Model solves energy transport equations simultaneously in fluid and solid domains, with heat exchange at every fluid-solid interface computed automatically. This means thermal gradients in a die wall due to spray cooling, the transient heat buildup during repeated casting cycles, and the temperature-dependent solidification of a melt are all resolved in a single simulation without manual coupling between separate solvers.

Heat transfer coefficients between different media can be either specified directly or calculated automatically based on the local flow conditions. A wide variety of boundary conditions are available to precisely control how heat enters and leaves a domain: specified heat flux, power source, prescribed temperature, convective heat transfer to an external environment, and radiative heat exchange with surrounding surfaces and voids. These thermal inputs can be controlled via Active Simulation Control.

Material properties such as density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, and surface tension can be specified in tabular form. This eliminates the need to fit experimental data to analytical functions, allowing complex, non-linear property dependencies to be represented directly from laboratory measurements.

*Temperature distribution in an aluminum HPDC casting during mold filling, showing conjugate heat transfer between the melt and surrounding die geometry.*
heading: Heat Transfer Model > Modeling Capabilities

text:
Heat Transfer Model > Phase Change

The Heat Transfer Model is the foundation for all phase change processes in the ***FLOW-3D*** product family. Liquid-solid phase change governs metal solidification and melting in casting, additive manufacturing, and welding applications. Liquid-vapor phase change governs boiling, evaporation, spray cooling, and cryogenic propellant behavior. Both phase change modes are tightly coupled to the energy transport equations so that latent heat, temperature-dependent solidus and liquidus lines, and enthalpy changes are all accounted for consistently.
heading: Heat Transfer Model > Phase Change

text:
Heat Transfer Model > Viscous Heating

In high-speed viscous flows, the dissipation of kinetic energy into heat can be significant. Viscous heating can be included in the energy transport equation for applications where this effect matters, such as polymer processing, high-speed lubrication flows, and non-Newtonian fluid handling.
heading: Heat Transfer Model > Viscous Heating

text:
Heat Transfer Model > Applications

The Heat Transfer Model is used across the ***FLOW-3D*** product family for:

- Metal casting thermal analysis, die temperature distribution, and thermal die cycling
- Additive manufacturing melt pool thermal evolution, heat affected zone prediction, and layer-by-layer thermal accumulation
- Laser welding thermal fields, keyhole dynamics, and heat affected zone characterization
- Spray and jet cooling of hot surfaces in industrial thermal management applications
- Buoyancy-driven flows in environmental and process engineering applications
- Boiling, evaporation, and condensation in chemical process and energy system modeling
- Conjugate heat transfer in heat exchangers, electronic cooling, and thermal management devices
- Cryogenic propellant tank pressurization and thermal stratification
- Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning

Validation of FLOW-3D against a 3D Dam Breaking Problem 
Peter Arnold, Minerva Dynamics, The Guildhall, High Street Bath, UK  
Introduction 
A 3D dam breaking with obstacle configuration was chosen as one of our FLOW-3D1 validation cases in order to 
assess FLOW-3D’s performance for the simulation of free-surface flows. The problem is well documented and 
easy to set up with all the experimental data generated available to download from the ERCOFTAC database[1]. 
The obstacle is chosen to be representative of a container exposed to green water on the deck of a ship. Videos 
of the experiment and SPH simulations (smoothed particle hydrodynamics) are available in the database that 
show impressive qualitative agreement. The experiment consists of a large tank 3.22m x 1m x 1m with a sliding 
door holding back 0.55m of water. The door is opened vertically upwards by a falling weight and the water is 
released to impinge on the obstacle and then be reflected from the tank walls 3 times. The free-surface 
elevation is measured at four locations along the center line of the tank and eight pressure sensors are 
embedded in the leading vertical and horizontal surfaces of the obstacle. CFD simulations using FLOW-3D v9.4 
were carried out on a series of progressively finer meshes and using different order numerical schemes and 
turbulence models.

Simulation Methodology 
The 3D dam breaking problem was originally developed by Kleefsman et al. [2.] Full details of the locations of the 
sensors and the experimental data and videos of the experiment and an SPH simulation are available in the EROFTAC 
validation database [1]. The simulation is carried out for a total of 6 seconds of real time. 
The FLOW-3D simulations were set up for a domain of 3.22m x 1m X 1.5m, i.e., 0.5 larger in the z-direction to allow 
any vertical jets of fluid to be captured (in the experiment the tank roof is open to atmosphere). The default mesh had 
hexahedral cells with a spacing of 161 in the x-direction, 50 in the y-direction and 75 in the z-direction and was 
uniformly spaced other than for accommodating fixed points to coincide with the obstacle and sensor locations, hence 
a total of approximately 603,750 cells. The obstacle was put into the domain and all walls were treated as no slip. 
After prescribing the initial location of the water and its viscosity, laminar time-dependent simulations were carried 
out for a series of progressively finer meshes starting from the default 603K cell mesh (Mesh 1). The approach taken 
was simply to increase the total cell count by a factor of two for each progressive mesh by increasing the number of 
cells in each direction by the cube root of 2. Four meshes were generated in this way, i

After prescribing the initial location of the water and its viscosity, laminar time-dependent simulations were carried 
out for a series of progressively finer meshes starting from the default 603K cell mesh (Mesh 1). The approach taken 
was simply to increase the total cell count by a factor of two for each progressive mesh by increasing the number of 
cells in each direction by the cube root of 2. Four meshes were generated in this way, i.e., Mesh 1, Mesh 2, Mesh 3 
and Mesh 4. The time histories of the free-surface elevation at four locations and the pressure from the eight pressure 
sensors were then plotted against the experimental data. The CPU and elapsed time of the four processors was also 
recorded. 
Using only Mesh 1, the effects of the numerical differencing scheme used for the momentum advection was 
investigated. The default 1st order, a 2nd order montonicity preserving and a 3rd order scheme were all used and the 
results compared. Also the effects of running in single and double precision were compared. Finally a mesh was 
designed ( Mesh 5) to capture the velocity gradient along the bottom wall and the bulk flow in the most active parts of 
the domain using 2.7 X 106 active cells. 
The turbulent fluctuations were modeled primarily by direct simulation, however, we have also included the results 
from two of the turbulence models available in FLOW-3D, i.e., the Renormalization Group (RNG) Model and the Large 
Eddy Simulations (LES ) model. All models were run on the coarsest mesh, i.e., Mesh 1 only. We have not attempted to 
satisfy the usual turbulence model associated constraints on the distance of the nearest node from the tank walls due 
to the excessive demands this would put on the mesh resolution. Also as the flow is largely chaotic and the obstacle is 
sharp edged the prediction of the flow separation effects will be driven by the rapid changes in geometry rather than 
by a gradual separation of an orderly boundary layer. Consequently, we have assumed that resolution of the boundary 
layer is less relevant than resolving the flow in the interior of the domain from the viewpoint of predicting the main 
flow features.

Free-Surface Elevation Results 
Figures 3-6 show the free-surface elevation plotted against time at each of the four locations with H4 being nearest 
and H1 being furthest from the original water column. It is encouraging for the validation that the main features are 
represented very well albeit with some differences in magnitude and timing. However, it must also be said that the 
experimental data has no error bars supplied with it and that the measurement of the free-surface elevation using 
probes in such a chaotic and separated flow field is likely to be problematic as the free-surface elevation may not be a 
single valued function of time. This probably accounts for the discrepancy in the H1 heights during the initial steep rise 
phase at around 1 second. The remainder of the H1 record is in good agreement with the experiments. The H2 plot 
shows even better agreement particularly in the initial water rising phase and predicts well the eventual maximum 
height of the water. The H3 plot again picks up the main characteristics but clearly shows a time lag between the 
simulations and experiment. The H4 plot shows excellent agreement in the initial phase as the water level is 
decreasing but underestimates the steepness and final values of the rise of the water column as it returns off the left 
and right hand walls respectively. 
The time lag feature of the simulations behind the experiment is present in all the plots and is also seen in the original 
CFD simulation by Kleefsman et al. [2] using their CoMFLOW code on a 236 X 76 X 68 grid and so cannot be attributed 
to FLOW-3D alone. The origin of the lag is unclear but it seems to be introduced gradually over the simulation.

Pressure Sensors Results 
Figures 7-10 show the four front face pressure sensors plotted against time, indicating generally good agreement 
between experiment and the simulations with the accuracy increasing for the pressure sensors located towards the 
floor of the tank. The P1 sensor estimates the arrival and magnitude of the pressure peak the most accurately. There is 
a considerable amount of fluctuation in the pressure signal between its arrival and about 2 seconds as the water 
rebounds from the obstacle and left wall after which the signal settles down and the simulations values agree well 
with the experimental values. Also the magnitude of the peak decrease with the height up the face of the sensor. The 
worst agreement occurs as we would expect at the P4 location where flow separation is taking place. 
Figures 11-14 show the top horizontal face pressure sensors, i.e., P5 to P8 also show along with experimental data, 
large fluctuations in pressure between 1 and 2 seconds after which again the simulations and experimental data settle 
down and agreement is improved. The CoMFLOW simulations performed by Kleefsman et al. [2] show similar 
characteristics and levels of agreement but overestimate the pressure peaks along the top face considerably more.

Mesh Refinement 
In terms of the effect of mesh refinement there seems to be little evidence that the solution is converging to a unique 
solution. This is perhaps not surprising as we have attempted to model the turbulence in the flow field by direct 
simulation instead of using a turbulence model. Using this approach we would expect the time-dependent solution to 
uncover more detail in the flow field as the mesh is refined and to become more sensitive to perturbations in the 
initial conditions. Also we would expect the average of many simulations with slightly different initial conditions to 
converge to an ensemble averaged solution with mesh refinement. However, in terms of the level of agreement with 
experiment there is little difference between the least and most expensive solutions which took approximately 35 
times longer. From an engineering perspective the coarsest mesh solution, i.e., Mesh 1 would be sufficiently accurate 
and represents very good value considering the elapsed simulation was only just over 15 minutes.

Conclusion 
FLOW-3D has been used to simulate a very challenging free-surface flow problem and has produced good qualitative 
and quantitative agreement with the experimental data. The main discrepancies could easily be due to problems 
measuring the free-surface elevation of what is at times a non-unique parameter. The prediction of pressure on the 
surface of an obstacle on which the flow impinges is also generally in good agreement with the experimental 
measurement, the main deviation being again where there is a significant amount of fluctuation in the experimental 
measurements. The repeatability of the experimental measurements has not been discussed in the literature but is 
likely to be at least as large as the differences in the CFD simulations. We have also found that the solution can be 
adequately obtained on a relatively coarse mesh using 1st order differencing with no turbulence model in around 15 
minutes on a shared memory configuration over four processors. The lack
